title: The Care-Full Study: A systems approach to older adults with multiple long term conditions' home-based care: mapping, scoping, feasibility, and modelling of factors affecting outcomes for unpaid caregiving
abstract: Aim To create knowledge and develop an innovation hub partnership focussed on delivering interventions to improve outcomes for unpaid carers and the older people with multiple conditions for whom they care  Background 1.5 million older people are estimated to have unmet need from state care provision, which is expected to more than double by 2051. Unpaid carers often meet this gap and 1 in 5 adults in the UK are carers. Caring can be rewarding but also brings health and financial challenges. Unpaid carers of older people with multiple conditions carry out complex care work, are the first point of call in an emergency, but are less likely to receive support than other types of carers. This proposed partnership brings system engineers, unpaid carers, older people, and care providers together to develop understanding and translate real-world information into unpaid caring system models. Possible uses of models include proactive identification of unpaid carers at risk of adverse outcomes and predictive modelling to support the carer decision-making for complex situations.  Activity  Over 18-months we will carry out 2 work packages (WPs), involving unpaid carers as peer researchers to maximise patient and public involvement. WP1 uses different methods across 2 workstreams (WS') to create an in-depth understanding of the experience and current context of unpaid caring and identify appropriate tools to measure the impact of unpaid care WS1: Creating a visual map of the current context of home-based care Participatory workshops involving unpaid carers and care providers to co-create a visual representation of the people, systems, and risk factors that impact unpaid carers, which will inform WP2 WS2: Developing an understanding of the types, availability, and accessibility of information and outcomes in current care systems  This will identify: 1) Key types and sources of data that document experiences, interventions, and outcomes related to unpaid carers  2) How possible collecting data over 12-month study is with 15 unpaid carer/older people pairs. Peer researchers will support data collection. Distinct from data collection, two coaching sessions will be offered to participants for more mutuality and equity. WP2: Building prototype systems models to identify links between the experiences and outcomes of unpaid carers and older people, to inform optimal service delivery and shape better outcomes  Systems modelling will use WP1 data to build models that identify what most influences decision-making in this complex care system, enabling suggestions for the best course of action even amid significant uncertainty, risk and complexity. These models will be presented to key stakeholders for initial feedback, building further data for the CARE-Full innovation hub application.  Developing the evidence and strategic partnerships Meetings with all stakeholders over the course of the study will support the continuous cycle of learning, development and co-created outputs. Outputs for hub development include: creating systems models for unpaid caring and identifying how to scale up models with more data; understanding of the types and feasibility of data that can be collected to scale in the Hub; building a strong hub partnership team around the experiences and important connections for unpaid carers and older people; disseminating co-produced (with peer researchers and strategic partners) research outputs on aspects of the partnership methods and findings.

title: Application Development Award   Image and Performance Enhancing Drugs (IPEDs): Assessment of available intelligence and research gaps to inform intervention evaluation
abstract: The use of anabolic androgenic steroids (AAS) and other image and performance enhancing drugs (IPEDs) is well-established within medicine as enhancement drugs in sport and increasingly in wider society. Use of AAS (the most commonly used IPED) is not confined to any specific community, socioeconomic group or ethnicity but is most commonly used by men between the age of 20 and 40 years.  Use of AAS causes damage to the heart, liver and brain, and imbalances in hormones, impacting on mood, sex drive, acne and baldness and is linked to depression, aggression and dependence. For men, hormonal imbalance may result in shrinkage of the testicles, and the development of female breast tissue in women, effects may be permanent including increased body hair, deepening of the voice, enlargement of the clitoris and menstrual irregularities leading to sterility. Illegal production of IPEDS leads to poor quality, unsterile products with unpredictable adverse effects. As many of these drugs are injected, there are risks of blood borne virus transmission with levels of HIV and hepatitis C higher than in the general population.  While the most common reason for IPED use is to increase lean muscle, many people have multiple motivations related to appearance, sport, sex drive or occupation. There are diverse groups of users, with varied characteristics, often related to these specific motivations.  There is a lack of evidence relating to interventions to reduce harms, support cessation of use or discourage use amongst those contemplating the use of IPEDs. To develop this evidence, we must first answer these fundamental questions:    How many IPED users are there in the UK and are there regional variations use? (WP1);    What is the current status  and focusof research in relation to IPEDs in the UK? (WP2);    What are the services and interventions for IPED users in the UK? (WP3);    What are the key factors that may influence decisions to use IPEDs? (WP4);   Alongside this we will:    Develop mechanisms to disseminate the findings of the research and further develop the current network   Anabolic Steroids UK (WP5).  The ASUK network will be essential for the consultation elements required to gain a consensus on how many AAS users there are in the UK (WP1). The network will be used to help identify and access recent UK literature (WP2) and will support the collection of research plans. Similarly, the ASUK Network will facilitate data collection on services providing interventions for IPED users (WP3) and enable recruitment of stakeholders for workshops to produce the systems mapping in relation to how individuals make decision on IPED use (WP4).  This research will have both short- and long-term impacts, providing vital information to support applications to the IPED evaluation of effectiveness call in 2021. This research will enable the first UK estimates of the extent of AAS to be calculated, with additional estimates produced at regional levels. The research will provide the evidence base relating to the current IPED research and the types and distribution of interventions for IPED users in the UK. Collaborative work with stakeholders will inform our understanding of the complex factors that influence the use of AAS and other IPEDs. In addition to traditional high-quality academic outputs of findings, the development of the ASUK Network and accompanying website will facilitate the dissemination of all research findings, ensuring maximum impact.

title: Models of social care provision and prison: Preparatory work for a mixed methods study
abstract: Background  Against a background of concern about a lack of social care in prisons, the introduction of the 2014 Care Act clarified the responsibility of local authorities for the social care needs of people in custody and on release.  However, whilst high levels of social care need have been found in the prison population (particularly amongst prisoners aged 50 and over and younger prisoners with accompanying mental health, learning or social communication difficulties), there has been remarkably little research on the best way to meet these. In the absence of this, significant variation has been reported in the emerging service delivery models and the number of people deemed to have eligible needs. We intend to prepare a programme grant (PG) application to address these issues through the development, delivery and evaluation of models of social care to meet the needs of prisoners following remission to prison and later release into the community. Before this work can be undertaken however some preparatory stages are required which are described in this development grant (PDG) application.  Objectives    Build the research team and required collaborations,  Develop understanding of the important social care practice issues and challenges, the wider context, system properties and the potential for change,  Identify the potential outcome measures to be used in the subsequent PG,  Establish what routinely collected data is available in the proposed study sites,  Synthesise the existing evidence on the provision of social care for people in custody,  Extend our existing review for people on release to incorporate relevant learning from studies of other client groups   Methods  Team Strengthening and Collaboration Building  This work package (WP) will build on our existing expertise through the fostering of collaborative networks and further training. It will also involve the recruitment of two groups, an advisory group and expert reference group, including experts by lived experience, who will be consulted throughout the project.  Methodological Work  The focus of this WP is on the use of a consensus approach to identify appropriate core outcome measures for prisoners on remission and later release, and then a review of data that is currently routinely collected on a national level.  Evidence Synthesis  The final WP will comprise a realist review and synthesis that will allow us to build on existing knowledge to develop an appropriate program theory to meet social care needs throughout the criminal justice system.  This PDG will provide a strong foundation for the proposed PG which will:     Develop, pilot, trial and establish the cost effectiveness of a service delivery model for the provision of social care in prison,  Develop a flexible service delivery model for the provision of social care for people released from prison that is ready for pilot testing with a longitudinal study   Conclusion  Improved social care will allow individuals to better engage with the prison regime and with society on release with benefits in terms of support and social engagement for individual prisoners, their families and ultimately wider society.

title: Inflammatory drivers of long-term comorbidity trajectories: an AI investigation of mulitimorbidity (inflAIM)
abstract: About 25% of the UK population have two or more long term conditions. This multimorbidity is associated with a reduction in quality of life, increased use of health services and reduced life expectancy. To date, multimorbidity has been seen as a random assortment of diseases, making it difficult to address. However, with new understanding of the impact of various factors (including biological, social, behavioural, environmental and others), multimorbidity can be seen as a series of non-random clusters of disease. Improving the characterisation of these clusters with artificial intelligence and machine learning could have significant benefits to health and social care.  In preparation for this development award we have assembled a team of computer and data scientists, statisticians, epidemiologists and clinicians with skills and interests in data analysis and interpretation, to address how to apply artificial intelligence (AI) methodology to develop new insights into the detection and prevention of multimorbid conditions.  Our focus will be on detecting long-term trajectories as they evolve over the life course by applying a combination of traditional methods and novel AI approaches under development by our group including probability (fuzzy) clustering and multistate modelling embedded in a deep learning framework.  As a paradigm, we will focus our analysis on the role of chronic inflammation in explaining the occurrence of disease across the life course. We will explore the informativeness of three test datasets where relevant long-term data on inflammatory exposures is recorded and test the feasibility of these methods in a set of proof of concept analyses. Chronic inflammation is an established driver of disease risk that is amenable to intervention and understanding its role in the evolution of multimorbidity provides a direct pathway to patient benefit.  By establishing a group of experts in clinical medicine, biological sciences, epidemiology, computing sciences  and statistics to bring a focus on inflammatory drivers of comorbidity, we expect this development work to demonstrate the feasibility of novel AI technologies to identify inflammation driven clustering of patient disease trajectories over a long time horizon.  We have significant research infrastructure partners (MRC Dementias Platform UK, NIHR Applied Research Collaboration Eastern), commercial advisors (British Telecom Health, Aviva Life Analytics, Evergreen Life and Vitality) and will have support and input from the Institute and Faculty of Actuaries.  These collaborations will enable us to scale up the analysis to include further local and national research and administrative databases in a future application.  By embedding patients in this project, and establishing an AI patient and public engagement group to assist with the understanding of the use of AI in data interpretation, we aim to ensure that the overarching aim of this work is to lead to effective strategies for disease prevention both for the benefit of individuals and for the population.

These collaborations will enable us to scale up the analysis to include further local and national research and administrative databases in a future application. By embedding patients in this project, and establishing an AI patient and public engagement group to assist with the understanding of the use of AI in data interpretation, we aim to ensure that the overarching aim of this work is to lead to effective strategies for disease prevention both for the benefit of individuals and for the population.

title: Pre-clinical testing of a real-time computer-assisted surgical navigation system
abstract: Navigating surgical tools and implants into the correct position when there is limited line-of-sight or surgical access significantly improves the outcome of many surgical procedures, including maxillofacial, cranial, spinal, and joint replacement surgeries4,5,6,7,8. However, all current surgical navigation technologies are invasive, due to the attachment of tracking markers to the patient s bone, which can result in bone fractures in up to 10% of cases9,10,11. Additionally, they require extensive operator training7,12,13 and significantly increase the operative time (20%~30 minutes)12,13.  C-True has developed a functional prototype of a non-invasive, marker-free navigation system that eliminates the need for attaching invasive markers, which greatly reduces surgical time and training required (Fig1-left). We achieved this by combining AI for anatomical recognition, 3D-depth cameras for spatial data acquisition, and advanced image registration algorithms. Our technology can be applied to various surgical fields, but we are currently focusing on Total Shoulder Replacement (TSR) due to its poor outcomes and high revision rates in the UK (11%~1000 revisions/year)14. We have conducted a global freedom-to-operate search in collaboration with patent attorneys and will protect intellectual property through a combination of trade secrets and patentable hardware.  The current sterilisable prototype has been validated in laboratory settings and has achieved state-of-the-art navigation accuracy of 1.3mm in translation and 1.8° in rotation, based on tests on 40 synthetic bones with anatomical variations (Fig1-right). However, further testing in realistic environments is required to bridge the evidence gap and demonstrate that the device can achieve the same level of accuracy in surgical settings.  Patient engagement is a priority to us. A patient advisory group of 5 members helped define the project and will continue to aid the team in determining priorities. Progress will be shared with the public through NHS-PPI sessions at Imperial College, ensuring patient perspectives and needs are considered throughout the process.

title: Evaluating Models of care, best practice and care pathways for women who are dependent on drugs and their infants, from preconception to 18 months postnatal
abstract: WHY DO WE NEED THIS STUDY?     Pregnant women and mothers who use drugs often have complex needs linked to past abuse, mental health problems, poor physical health, drug-related violence and crime, exclusion, homelessness and poverty. Babies born to mothers who use drugs sometimes require treatment for drug withdrawal symptoms after they are born, experience problems with their early health and development, and are more likely to be taken into care within the first two years of life. Although there are various guidelines on the care of pregnant women and mothers who use drugs, and policies which encourage health and social care services to work together to support women, we know very little about the sorts of services that are available in the UK, whether these services meet the needs of women and infants, whether they are acceptable to women, and whether they lead to better or worse outcomes for families. This study will try to answer these questions through a detailed study of women's experiences of health and social care from early pregnancy to two years after the baby is born.     WHAT WILL THE STUDY INVOLVE?     1.An 'expert advisory group' made up of services users and professionals will be set up to work with the research team throughout the project - providing information, advice and feedback on all aspects of the research.   2. A review of books, reports and articles on ways of providing care for pregnant women and two years after a baby is born will be carried out to see what works, why, for whom, and under what circumstances. We will then examine best practice by reviewing documents for professionals (clinical guidelines, treatment protocols and good practice guidance). We will use these two reviews to decide what kind of services, interventions and approaches to care are best suited to this group of mothers and infants, and to improve outcomes for mum, baby and the family as a whole.   3.We will explore women's experiences of care, and their care journey, from pregnancy to two years after the birth. If COVID restrictions continue, the study will take place remotely in interviews and conversations with women by mobile phone calls, texts and video calls with women to hear about their experiences of care. We will also interview staff (midwives, doctors, substance use workers, social workers), managers and commissioners. This will be carried out in four areas (two in Scotland, two in England) that have different ways of providing care, cultures, types of drug use, and health and social care policies. We will recruit 40 women at different stages of care and work with them over an 18- month period..     HOW WILL THE STUDY BENEFIT WOMEN, INFANTS, FAMILIES AND SOCIETY?   The study will try to establish the best way of providing care for women who use drugs, from pregnancy to eighteen months after the birth of their baby, which meets the needs of women and achieves the best outcomes for children, families and society as a whole. Our study is important for several policies in the UK: Improving the way care is provided to pregnant women and mothers; Improving the health and development of children affected by parental substance use and other negative experiences; changing the way health and social care is provided to reduce inequalities, and: Involving patients and the public in redesigning services. More information can be found at https://www.kcl.ac.uk/research/the-stepping-stones-study

title: Intelligent prediction of preterm birth using AI-empowered electrohysterography sensing
abstract: Background Preterm birth increases not only the risks of neonatal mortality, but numerous health risks for surviving babies. Pregnant women have been defined by the NIHR as an under-served group whose inclusion needs to be improved in clinical research.The public sector costs of preterm delivery in England and Wales have been estimated at Â£3.4bn annually. Prediction of preterm birth is crucial to deliver interventions that are time-dependent for neonatal survival. The main device currently available for routine uterine contraction detection is the tocodynamometer (TOCO), which suffers from several drawbacks and provides limited information for the prediction of premature birth. The more comfortable technique called electrohysterograhy (EHG) offers an alternative for uterine contraction monitoring. Aims and Objectives Using available EHG signals from existing datasets (one online database, one from our previous research), we aim to develop an AI solution to: 1) translate EHG to TOCO-like waveforms that could help facilitate the clinical acceptance for EHG adoption into maternal monitoring practice; and 2) predict preterm birth by an AI algorithm. Work plan, methods and timelines The project has four work packages: 1) Develop TOCO-like waveform generation algorithm based on wavelet and Independent Component Analysis using online database (Months 1-4) 2) Develop an AI algorithm to predict preterm labour based on Dictionary Learning and Sparse Representation using online database (Months 4-10) 3) Pre-clinical efficacy test using our independent database (Months 10-12) 4) Co-creation with key stakeholders to determine their requirements and market analysis (Months 1-12) Anticipated Impact and Dissemination Our proposed technology is ultimately anticipated to reduce neonatal mortality, improve patient outcome and experience, and to save costs for the NHS. Follow-up work will include further development and clinical evaluation of the technology, in collaboration with health economists, clinicians and commercial partners to support future implementation and dissemination of our technology.

title: NIHR Global Health Research Group on Digital Diagnostics for African Health Systems
abstract: Aims of the research:   We want to investigate whether a new type of diagnostic test, called a digital diagnostic, will be better than currently available diagnostic tests in African health care settings. We want to look at this in scenarios where there are important gaps in the availability, accuracy, or data collection from current diagnostic tests. These scenarios are: 1. detection of malaria parasites; 2. Cause of fever in young children; 3. detecting bacterial contamination of water and food.     Background to the research:   Making the correct diagnosis when someone is ill ensures they receive the right treatment and have the best chance of getting better. In rich countries it is taken for granted that when someone is ill, all of the tests that are needed can be performed to reach a diagnosis. In much of Africa, most people do not have access to essential diagnostic tests, either because they live too far away from the relatively few laboratories that can offer these tests or because they cannot afford them. As a result most treatment is based on informed guesswork of the most likely cause. This results in overuse of antibiotics and antimalarial drugs, which in turn favours the development of resistance.     We have developed a digital diagnostic device, called Lacewing, which makes diagnoses by detecting tiny molecules from a drop of blood or saliva on the surface of a microchip and generates electronic signals. These signals are transmitted to a smartphone and give the user a diagnosis. Because the  lab-on-chip  does all of the work, the technology is very easy to use and enables very accurate diagnosis to be made by rapidly by a cheap, robust and fully portable handheld device. This means that the capability of an advanced diagnostic lab can now be taken to the patient.              Design and methods used:   We want to understand whether the Lacewing diagnostic will work properly, whether it will provide accurate diagnoses, and whether we can optimise it to give the maximum chance that it is adopted into practice in African healthcare systems. To do this, we need to fully understand the context in which it will be used, and understand the perspectives of all of those who might be impacted, from the patients and healthcare workers right up to ministries of health and international policy makers. We do this through different types of interviews and focus groups. We optimise the design of Lacewing in partnership with the intended users   so called  co-design . We assess the potential impact on health systems to understand how other aspects of diagnosis and care might be affected. We compare accuracy of diagnoses using Lacewing against those of the best possible "gold standard" diagnostic tests, and also against any tests in common use in Africa.       Community Engagement and Involvement:   The involvement of community members, as potential end-users of the diagnostics, is central to the co-design process. Wider community engagement will be undertaken for the diagnostic accuracy studies to ensure that the research is appropriate and approved by the local communities.       Dissemination:  Dissemination is an essential component of our work. We want to share our results widely with communities in Africa, with policy makers, and with the commercial sector. We will do this using creative tools, videos and demonstrations, to raise awareness of the potential of digital diagnostics to transform health care in Africa.

title: Supporting the spread of effective integration models for older people living in care homes: A mixed method approach
abstract: Research question: The project seeks to identify, classify and compare the types and extent of locally-implemented integrated care policies in relation to care homes in England.  Background: Closer integration of social care and health services is a policy priority in many countries. The NHS Long Term Plan committed to rolling-out innovative integration practices across England with a specific emphasis on initiatives aimed at care home residents. However, the optimal mix of integration care home initiatives, when and in what context is unknown. Comprehensive knowledge of existing integrated initiatives, their types, the factors which enable or hamper implementation and their effect on key outcomes is key to supporting their efficient and effective, national roll-out.   Aims and objectives: We will create an online  policy extraction and mapping  tool that allows commissioners, advocates of potential/current care-users and researchers to examine the presence and extent of local care home integration interventions across England. Data will be summarised in accessible ways to rank localities across multiple domains of integration and to examine the association of these domains with key indicators of social care and health system performance, with care home market characteristics and local authorities  procurement strategies being mediating/moderating factors. Findings will empower: i) care service users /relatives  decision-making, through transparent and accessible information; ii) local commissioners, by better shared learning on best practices; iii) national decision-makers, to track the progress of integration and to support the scale-up of best-practice; and iv) researchers, by enabling comparison of locally implemented integration interventions implemented.  Methods: We will identify integration interventions referenced in official documents by customising and using existing artificial intelligence methods (text mining and machine learning). The information we collect will be synthesised in a  policy map  (grid of interventions by locality and year), validated by researchers during piloting, and by a national survey about local policymaker activity. We will construct a  diagnostic  index of integration using latent factor structural equation models, validated by panel discussions with experts and PPI/E representatives. We will investigate the relationships between local contextual and care market factors, the extent of integration and key social care and health systems performance indicators using multivariate regression models.  Timelines for delivery: The project will be delivered in 24 months, including an initial 6 months piloting in Greater Manchester with results disseminated in month 7, and subsequent national scale-up, with results disseminated in months 13, 20, 21 and 24.     Anticipated impact and dissemination: Decision-makers, provider organisations, local community groups and also individual service users and carers must consider carefully how to make informed use of the resources available to them. We will consult with them to maximise impact and disseminate results effectively in a variety of formats. Our outcomes will: i) promote informed decision-making and incentivise best-practice; ii) track changes in integration to support national roll-out; iii) support local authorities in  market shaping  and in 'fostering  service quality; iv) provide evidence on the optimal mix of integration activities that maximise improvements in residents  outcomes.

title: Development and validation of prediction models for secukinumab therapy in psoriasis: a machine learning approach enabling personalised medicine
abstract: Research question Can machine learning methods identify clinical markers predictive of secukinumab treatment response? Background Psoriasis is a chronic, immune-mediated disease with significant associated comorbidities. The use of high-cost biologics have revolutionised treatment of psoriasis, however only around 50% of patients with psoriasis will remain on a biologic for 3 years due to loss of effectiveness. Little is known about what predicts variability in biologic treatment response. Despite extensive research using genetic and molecular biomarkers, there are currently no predictors accurate enough for use in clinical practice.  Recent advances in data science have led to breakthroughs in machine learning with potential to discover insights into underlying structures of large and complex datasets. Secukinumab (IL-17A inhibitor) is one of the current leading choice of biologics for psoriasis, which has been studied in the largest cohort of randomised controlled trials (RCTs). The British Association of Dermatologists Biologics and Immunomodulators Register (BADBIR) is the largest psoriasis and pharmacovigilance registry in the world. We propose a unique opportunity to apply state-of-the-art machine learning approaches to interrogate these high-quality resources.  The central hypothesis of this project is that baseline clinical characteristics can be used to predict treatment response to secukinumab in psoriasis.  Aims I aim to take an unsupervised, data-driven approach to identify baseline clinical predictors associated with responses to secukinumab treatment. To accomplish these aims, I will receive further training from leading data science teams in Manchester, Newcastle and industry to develop expertise in machine learning methods. (Months 0-6)  Methods. (Months 6-12) I will use secukinumab RCTs as a training dataset to develop predictive models. (Months 12-18) I will apply latent class longitudinal analysis to investigate whether patients can be divided into distinct groups according to the trajectory of change in psoriasis clearance following secukinumab therapy. (Months 18-24) I will apply different risk prediction methods (support vector machine and random forests) to classify baseline clinical characteristics, mapped to the response trajectories, to discriminate long-term treatment responder and non-responder. (Months 24-30) I will develop a web-based prognostic calculator and validate using data from real-world psoriasis registry (BADBIR).  Summary  Using machine learning to inform clinical predictors could improve classification of treatment responders for better treatment stratification in the management of psoriasis patients. This may potentially shift the current biologic prescribing paradigm in psoriasis.  Impact.  This project aligns well with the NIHR's Academy strategic theme for Health Data Science to deliver precision medicine through data. It is ambitious, but will take maximal advantage from the research partnership between the Universities of Manchester-Newcastle-industry (Novartis); and equip me with high-level computational skills to become a future leader in this field. Patient groups have been involved in the inception and development of the project, providing constructive feedback to translate the findings into a web-based decision aid.  Dissemination.  I will ensure timely dissemination of results by publishing original research papers in high-impact journals, and presenting work at international meetings. I will make the codes and software developed open source; the methods would be of interest to a wide audience.

Background Psoriasis is a chronic, immune-mediated disease with significant associated comorbidities. The use of high-cost biologics have revolutionised treatment of psoriasis, however only around 50% of patients with psoriasis will remain on a biologic for 3 years due to loss of effectiveness. Little is known about what predicts variability in biologic treatment response. Despite extensive research using genetic and molecular biomarkers, there are currently no predictors accurate enough for use in clinical practice. Recent advances in data science have led to breakthroughs in machine learning with potential to discover insights into underlying structures of large and complex datasets. Secukinumab (IL-17A inhibitor) is one of the current leading choice of biologics for psoriasis, which has been studied in the largest cohort of randomised controlled trials (RCTs). The British Association of Dermatologists Biologics and Immunomodulators Register (BADBIR) is the largest psoriasis and pharmacovigilance registry in the world. We propose a unique opportunity to apply state-of-the-art machine learning approaches to interrogate these high-quality resources. The central hypothesis of this project is that baseline clinical characteristics can be used to predict treatment response to secukinumab in psoriasis. Aims I aim to take an unsupervised, data-driven approach to identify baseline clinical predictors associated with responses to secukinumab treatment. To accomplish these aims, I will receive further training from leading data science teams in Manchester, Newcastle and industry to develop expertise in machine learning methods. (Months 0-6) Methods. (Months 6-12) I will use secukinumab RCTs as a training dataset to develop predictive models. (Months 12-18) I will apply latent class longitudinal analysis to investigate whether patients can be divided into distinct groups according to the trajectory of change in psoriasis clearance following secukinumab therapy. (Months 18-24) I will apply different risk prediction methods (support vector machine and random forests) to classify baseline clinical characteristics, mapped to the response trajectories, to discriminate long-term treatment responder and non-responder. (Months 24-30) I will develop a web-based prognostic calculator and validate using data from real-world psoriasis registry (BADBIR). Summary Using machine learning to inform clinical predictors could improve classification of treatment responders for better treatment stratification in the management of psoriasis patients. This may potentially shift the current biologic prescribing paradigm in psoriasis. Impact. This project aligns well with the NIHR's Academy strategic theme for Health Data Science to deliver precision medicine through data. It is ambitious, but will take maximal advantage from the research partnership between the Universities of Manchester-Newcastle-industry (Novartis); and equip me with high-level computational skills to become a future leader in this field. Patient groups have been involved in the inception and development of the project, providing constructive feedback to translate the findings into a web-based decision aid. Dissemination. I will ensure timely dissemination of results by publishing original research papers in high-impact journals, and presenting work at international meetings. I will make the codes and software developed open source; the methods would be of interest to a wide audience.

title: Personalising azole antifungals and immunoglobulin therapies for haematopoietic stem cell transplantation and antibody deficient children using pharmacokinetic population models.
abstract: Background Personalised medicine can improve therapeutic management of individuals or a cohort. Patients with antibody deficiency(AD) and those undergoing haematopoietic stem cell transplantation(HSCT) require precise polypharmacy management to remain well. Antifungals, immunosuppression and immunoglobulin replacement are used to prevent life-threatening complications in these patients, but evidence to support precision dosing is lacking.  Azole antifungals(azoles) pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics(PKPD)  Itraconazole, posaconazole and voriconazole are used to prevent and treat invasive fungal diseases. Itraconazole and posaconazole lack paediatric licences, whereas voriconazole is licensed from >2 years of age. In 2018, we demonstrated that therapeutic posaconazole concentration was challenging to achieve in young children. Literature also describes difficulties in achieving therapeutic targets of other azoles.  Drug-drug interaction  CYP3A4 enzyme is responsible for adverse drug-drug interactions. CYP3A7 is expressed instead of CYP3A4 in infants up to 12 months of age. Most paediatric drug-drug interaction information is extrapolated from adult data. The differential expression and activity of these enzymes can significantly alter drug depositions in small children. This is particularly important in HSCT children who receive concurrent therapies(e.g. ciclosporin, azoles) metabolised by these enzymes.  Immunoglobulin in AD patients  The UK's immunoglobulin usage has been rationalised due to limited supply. The minimum immunoglobulin plasma level to prevent various infections in AD patients remains undefined. Optimising dosage and target level can help utilise immunoglobulin effectively.  Research questions   What is the optimal azoles dose for HSCT children?  How do azoles affect ciclosporin concentration quantitatively?  What is the optimal subcutaneous dose and lowest effective immunoglobulin plasma level to prevent infection in AD children?   GOSH parents reviewed this proposal and confirmed its relevance to patient care, contributed to plain English summary and result dissemination method.  Aims  To develop treatment algorithms for the optimum clinical dose regimens of studied medicines.  Objectives  To investigate the:   PKPD and dose of azoles(all administration routes)  age-stratified CYP3A-mediated drug interaction between ciclosporin and azoles quantitatively  optimal subcutaneous immunoglobulin dose and blood level to reduce infection risk  Method  Population PKPD non-linear mixed-effects models will be built. Retrospective patient data will be analysed to optimise pharmacotherapy in HSCT and AD children aged 0 to 18 years.  Delivery timelines  I will dedicate the first two years to research question 1 and 2 whilst adopting PKPD modelling and research skills and completing my clinical development courses. I will then apply my refined modelling skills to the third question in my third(final) year. I will meet with my supervisory team and patient involvement panel throughout my fellowship to review progress and seek feedback on results and future direction.  Anticipated impact and dissemination  Collaboration with the local teams will ensure the research results(new dosing and therapeutic-monitoring guidelines) be incorporated into patients' daily care. This project will feed into the national paediatric Antifungal Stewardship programme and UK Primary Immunodeficiency Network aiming to guide national prescribing in paediatrics. After implementation at local level, the effects of proposed models in practice will be investigated via an audit. Summary findings co-authored with parents representatives will be disseminate to public. Results will be publicised as peer-reviewed publications and in conferences.

title: Point-of-care Heart Failure Diagnosis for GP Use:  Implementation and Evaluation of a Simple AI-tool into the Folio of Care Pathways Serviced by Imperial's Connected Care National GP Network
abstract: This first real-world evaluation of a simple-to-use AI-tool for GP point-of-care diagnosis of heart failure (HF) builds on the track record of the Connected Care Bureau (CCB) in establishing impactful AI-enhanced pathways across a growing Connected Care GP network.   Consuming 2% of the entire NHS budget, 1M people in the UK have HF – increasing 50% by 2040. Although 40% of patients will have seen their GP with symptoms of HF, the high demand, the importance of accuracy, and its difficulty results in diagnosis per NICE guidelines in only 4% of patients. Consequently, 80% of HF is diagnosed only at life-threatening hospital admission, with 83% found to have the common form with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF).   The Eko DUO digitally-enhanced stethoscope and cloud-based convolutional neural network is capable of determining if a patient has clinically significant HFrEF, at the national guideline-indicated treatment threshold of 40% EF with 100% sensitivity and 80% specificity.    The project will apply the Eko DUO in easily implemented point-of-care diagnostic pathways over 12 months in 10 GP practices across two UK regions in 200 patients in whom the GP considers HFrEF as a possibility. All patients will also proceed through the established NHS pathway, with a repeat Eko DUO measurement performed for both direct correlation and reproducibility at the time of echocardiography - supplemented by real-world correlation with 300 unselected consecutive echos to explore refinements to diagnostic yield.     Accuracy of the Eko DUO, and the time to diagnosis and resource utilisation of the two pathways will be compared. The twin challenges of early diagnosis of HF and its undiagnosed prevalence in the general population are among the biggest facing the NHS and would be transformed by an effective point-of-care diagnostic and pathway, anticipating our Phase 4 and 5 applications to the AI Award towards adoption nationally.

title: Determining the Clinical Utility of Pre-emptive Pharmacogenetic Testing and Defining Optimal Models for Implementation
abstract: Medicines are the most common therapeutic intervention in healthcare, yet the efficacy and safety of many drugs show considerable inter-personal variation. Some patients are prescribed inefficacious medication, whereas others develop adverse drug reactions. This variation has a significant personal, clinical, and economic impact, leading to poorer individual and societal outcomes. Strategies are required to reduce this variability. One approach is to leverage knowledge of an individual's genetic information to support medicines optimisation, better informing medicine selection and dosing (pharmacogenetics). Evidence-based guidelines to support pharmacogenetic-guided prescribing are available for many commonly prescribed medicines. Despite a good understanding of these medicine-gene relationships, clinical implementation in the UK is limited to a small number of medicines. This is typically carried out reactively, where single genes are analysed when a medication is considered.  Given the high population frequency of genetic variation which influences the efficacy and safety of medicines, an alternative approach to pharmacogenetic guided prescribing is pre-emptive panel testing. This involves testing individuals for many common pharmacogenetic variants at a set time, irrespective of the medicine they are prescribed. This information can then be integrated into a patient's medical records and used to inform prescribing. I have developed three work-packages to determine the value of this pre-emptive approach to pharmacogenetic testing and to investigate how best to implement this in clinical practice.  I will first review the literature describing previous efforts to implement pre-emptive pharmacogenetic testing. This will be undertaken using the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research to characterise existing models and identify the determinants of successful clinical implementation.  Secondly, I will undertake a cross-sectional study linking patient genotype with prescribing data to measure the clinical utility of pre-emptive pharmacogenetic panel testing. In-patients (n=323) admitted to the Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust through the Acute Medical Unit and outpatients (n=323) in Genomic Medicine will be recruited. A DNA sample will be taken from each participant and tested using the AgenaTM iPLEX® PGx 74 and CYP2D6 copy number panels, covering the most relevant variants in 20 principal genes involved in drug metabolism. Inpatient and community prescribing data will be cross-referenced against patient genotype. The primary outcome is the proportion of patients with a genotype related to a medicine they are currently, or have previously been, prescribed. Genotype-phenotype relationships will be assigned where there is high level evidence for clinical actionability. This will determine the potential clinical value of the approach, both in the primary and secondary care settings.  Finally, I will undertake a stated preference study, employing a Discrete Choice Experiment (DCE), to identify clinical and non-clinical stakeholder preferences for the design of a pharmacogenetic service. A national sample of secondary care (n=150), primary care (n=150), and public stakeholders (n=300) will be recruited. The DCE will measure the relative value attached to factors influencing the design of a system to deliver pre-emptive pharmacogenetic testing.  Implemented effectively, pharmacogenetics has the potential to improve patient outcomes. The outputs from each of these work-packages will inform the development of a local and national pharmacogenetic service.

title: Feasibility study for the use of computer game base AI technology in the early diagnosis of Mild Cognitive Impairment Alzheimer's Disease
abstract: There is a chronic lack of an inexpensive, simple and effective way to accurately screen and diagnose Alzheimer s Disease:    Affecting 55Mn people globally[1], rising to over 150Mn by 2050[3].  41Mn people remain undiagnosed, hence no access to appropriate care[2].  In the UK at least 20% are diagnosed inaccurately[5]  Costing the global healthcare system $1Tn annually, tripling by 2030[3;7]  £34.7Bn UK alone, increasing to £94.1Bn by 2040[4].   Indicating massive and growing unmet need[1;6;7] to identify individuals easily and early to allocate management/care-resources accordingly.  Current gold-standard diagnostics are reliant on initial GP-screening then consequent multiple protracted clinical diagnostic examinations by numerous healthcare professionals.  These methods are highly resource intensive and expensive in terms of clinical time, effort, burden and complexity (need for multiple tests). For the patients these tests are also highly invasive (Spinal puncture, blood, PET and MRI scans), obviously daunting and suffer from a substantially growing waiting-list between initial GP-screening and eventual hospital diagnosis. Furthermore, accessibility; 52% fear diagnosis, 56% delay seeking diagnosis for up-to a year or more[8;9].  Current State-Of-The-Art[10;11;12;13] demand unfeasibly high user-motivation, attention, are symptom-based, lack evidence, require costly specialist hardware, installation, training, maintenance and multiple operators, proving ineffective.  We have developed a highly-innovative deep-learning-Artificial-Intelligence(AiaMD)-game-based proof-of-concept-TRL3-prototype currently being clinically validated. Targeting collaborator newly-discovered braincells that are the earliest affected by Alzheimers-Disease[14-High-Profile-Nature-Neuroscience] providing substantially earlier and much more accurate concurrent primary-care-GP-screening and secondary-care-diagnostics over anything currently available, potentially leading towards a world-first non-pharmacological treatment.  Current testing demonstrates substantially-higher efficacy (sensitivity and specificity) between healthy, early-Alzheimer s and mild-cognitively-impaired patients versus RAVLT, ACE3, MMSE and MoCA gold-standard clinical-tests in 3 separate gameplay-tests featuring 20 PPI and 18 clinical volunteers, informing test design/outcome measures and proving usability/effectiveness.  This project will confirm previous PPI software modifications and guide further development from our £300k IUK-Smart project ensuring optimal usability/end-user correctness of our videogame-prototype.

title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) Powered Psychosis Assessment Tool for Primary Care
abstract: Currently, Primary Care is expected to facilitate access to appropriate treatment for individuals experiencing "non-severe mental health conditions," such as anxiety or depression, while directing those with "severe mental health conditions" towards early intervention in psychosis (EIP) services. Nevertheless, in practice, General practitioners (GPs) are called upon to support individuals with psychosis, bipolar disorder, personality disorders, and other diverse and complex needs[1]. GPs often feel ill-equipped to address these varied challenges, and many lack prior experience in psychiatric services[2].  Psyrin is a cutting-edge Machine Learning algorithm (TRL 5, Tier C) grounded on the latest research evidence[3][4][5][6][7][8][9]to analyse over 150 features from a 5-minute speech sample. This comprehensive analysis, incorporating both linguistic and acoustic elements, enables Psyrin to accurately identify potential mental illnesses like schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, depression, and high psychosis risk. GPs could invite people to perform a speech test, and Psyrin will provide likelihood scores for each relevant mental illness to assist GPs in providing care and referrals effectively and timely.  We validated Psyrin in an Innovate UK-funded study collecting speech data from over 1100 individuals. We trained and tested our proprietary algorithm, which had 90% accuracy (macro recall = 0.89, macro precision = 0.92) in classifying individuals into healthy, at-risk, schizophrenia and bipolar groups.  We have conducted two Patient and Public Involvement, Engagement and Participation (PPIEP) workshops to gauge patient sentiments about recording their speech for potential assessment regularly. Patients expressed no concerns and preferred regular recordings for ease of recall. They also acknowledged the significance of the research and highlighted difficulties in navigating mental health care pathways, with half of them facing substantial challenges. We invited one PPIEP member who has experience of living with anxiety and depression, and have had challenges in accessing mental health support to review this proposal.

title: STIMULATE-ICP (Symptoms, Trajectory, Inequalities and Management: Understanding Long-COVID to Address and Transform Existing Integrated Care Pathways)
abstract: Background: Long COVID clinics are being implemented as usual care, but clinical characteristics, effective management strategies, recovery pathways, resource needs, and equitable access remain ill-defined.     Aim: To develop integrated care pathways (ICPs) for long COVID, and to evaluate effectiveness and cost-effectiveness, compared with usual care.     Methods: We will define optimal long COVID care pathways (investigation, treatment, rehabilitation) in an adaptive, 2-year programme with three work packages involving: long COVID clinics in six regions; patient support groups; policymakers; specialist health professionals and academics in long COVID and integrated care.     First, we will study patient trajectories, healthcare utilisation, effectiveness and cost of usual long COVID care using: (i)UK linked national records(n=56 million); (ii)prospective cohort study of non-hospitalised long COVID(n=500); (iii)long COVID clinics (n=6); (iv)qualitative interviews(n=30); and (v)”deep phenotyping”(e.g. omics, imaging, physiology) of common symptom groupings(n=300).     Second, in a pragmatic cluster (primary care network-level)-randomised trial, we will evaluate ICPs with early, supported investigation (multi-organ MRI with CoverscanTM and clinical decision support) and enhanced rehabilitation (Living with COVID RecoveryTM), compared with usual care(basic investigations and YourCOVIDRecoveryTM self-management), recruiting adults with suspected long COVID at referral(n=4520). In a nested, multi-arm, randomised (patient-level) drug trial, we will assess aspirin, colchicine and loratidine/famotidine versus standard of care. Primary outcome is fatigue assessment scale at three months. We will develop a long COVID core outcome dataset for research and assess cost-effectiveness of interventions.     Third, with patients, we will co-develop interventions (enhanced case-finding) to improve access to care and support. In long COVID clinics, our trials and national data, we will investigate inequalities by geographic location, socioeconomic status, ethnicity and pandemic stage.     Outputs for long COVID policy and research include: (i)evaluation of current care and clinical trajectory; (ii)effective and equitable care pathways, transferable to other long-term conditions; (iii)platform for future trials; and (iv)biobank for investigating outcome and treatment response(~5000).

title: Characterising the dynamic inter-relationships between polypharmacy and multiple long-term conditions.  Using artificial intelligence (AI) to map patient journeys into multimorbidity clusters across the UK
abstract: Overarching question: “How do polypharmacy and multiple long-term conditions (multimorbidity)(MLTC-M) interact and can enhanced understanding of their inter-relationships help to define optimised treatment strategies?”   Overarching aim: to better understand the complex interactions between polypharmacy and disease clustering over the life-course.  Our ultimate goal is to identify  tipping points  associated with progressive multimorbidity and polypharmacy which could trigger pre-emptive interventions.  Appropriately designed clinical decision support systems, including alerts for electronic health records (EHRs), would then inform patient-centered conversations around management options.     Background    MLTC-M is associated with premature mortality, significant treatment burden, increased healthcare and socio-economic costs.   Factors contributing to a trajectory of increasing multimorbidity remain to be defined.  Polypharmacy (defined as the simultaneous use of five or more medications) is associated with MLTC-M but their inter-relationship is poorly understood. Whereas appropriate polypharmacy may alleviate and/or prevent disease burden, inappropriate polypharmacy may do the reverse.   Access to data in EHRs and application of AI enables detailed study of the relationships between polypharmacy and MLTC-M over time, and in the context of other potential risk and protective factors.      Aims and objectives of Development Work    Establish a functional consortium including PPI groups, ensuring optimal membership and configuration.  Refine our data engineering, AI and machine learning methodology and develop working definitions of “polypharmacy”.  Perform an exploratory analysis to identify proof-of-principle clusters of MLTC-M associated with, and defined by links to polypharmacy.       Methods Building on our combined expertise in innovative healthcare data science, during the Development Award we will:    Establish data access, integration and sharing, across the two main centres, ensuring compliance with relevant governance standards.   Utilise clinical and prescription data within the UK Biobank to refine AI and machine learning methods and develop proof-of-principle MLTC-M/polypharmacy clustering outputs.    Establish access to anonymised EHR data in two geographically and demographically distinct, patient populations, in North East and North Cumbria and East London. These datasets, representing ethnically and socially diverse populations will provide the basis for the full Research Collaboration application.    Impacts The contrasting ethnicity but similar deprivation across our two populations offers a unique opportunity to study MLTC-M and polypharmacy in the context of these important risk factors.  The Development Award will position us to investigate these two populations with clearly defined, PPI and stakeholder informed, research questions and methodologies.   During the full Research Collaboration, we will define detailed patient journeys into MLTC-M, providing a deeper understanding of the inter-relationships with polypharmacy and other drivers (e.g. Black, Asian and Minority Ethnic populations). This will enable design of early warning and clinical decision support tools to flag risk to health professionals, pharmacists and patients. Identification of potential 'tipping  points will inform holistic, inclusive and patient-centered conversations around management options. We will use target trial emulation to analyse longitudinal routine data and to optimally design prospective pragmatic trials, relevant to the management of MLTC-M.   Dissemination Informed by consultation with our PPI groups, important findings and messages will be shared widely.  A methodological paper outlining our analysis plans will be published in a clinically impactful peer reviewed journal.

title: National evaluation of trials to test innovative early years workforce models
abstract: Background: The Family Hubs and Start for Life Programme Guidance (DHSC/DfE 2022) recommends increasing workforce capacity and capability through the use of new workforce models that incorporate skill mix. Evidence of the effectiveness of different early years workforce models, however, remains sparse, and the proposed research aims to address this gap.  Aims and objectives:  The overarching aim is to explore how skin mix models are working within the Start for Life Programme. The four objectives are as follow:  Objective 1: To map the workforce skill mix models in the five pilot Local Authorities (LAs) to act as a baseline for all later data collection. Objective 2: To identify the mechanisms by which the above models work, including identification of the processes supporting and preventing implementation of these models, across a range of different contexts Objective 3: To examine the structures and experiences of the networks between service users and providers within the different skill mix models. Objective 4: To establish the impact of the workforce models on key outcomes.  Methods: The evaluation is informed by Complexity Theory and a test-and-learn approach. All methods will be co-developed with a PPI lead and representative groups. Mapping (Objective 1): will involve the analysis of service and management information (MI) and interviews with key stakeholders to map the workforce models and understand how they are being implemented in the five pilot LA s. MI or survey information will be used to assess the extent to which the skill mix changes are different to the remaining 70 LA s.     Implementation (Objective 2): will identify the system-level mechanisms, facilitators and barriers for implementing the pilot models. Following the baseline mapping (Objective 1), ice cross-sectional workforce survey will be undertaken (with a later follow-up survey - optional costing), and desktop reviews of service and MI data will be carried out, each culminating in a multi-disciplinary workshop (the latter being an optional costing).  Experience and structures (Objective 3): will examine service user and provider experiences, and the structures that support effective working. Family-level case studies (N = 75) and Social Network Analysis will be used to examine the connections between professionals in the network around individual families, and the impact of those relationships on families  and professionals  experiences.   Impact (Objective 4): will involve Synthetic Control Methods to establish the impact of the workforce models on key outcomes including the quality and completion rate of the Healthy Child Programme, the 5 mandated health reviews, early identification of need and access to specialist services, safeguarding outcomes, disparities, workforce productivity and caseload, and cost effectiveness. This will involve the analysis of data from both national (e.g. Community Services Data Set) and local (e.g. social services) data.    Impact and dissemination: This research will provide much needed information about how early years workforce models can provide safe, high-quality, effective, and patient-centred services. Dissemination plans will be co-produced with families, identifying key audiences and channels, and leveraging maximum research impact through a range of methods including policy workshops, practice guidelines and parent-friendly information.

title: Prognostic models in rare diseases: methodology development with application to Ewing sarcoma
abstract: Research question How to develop prognostic models in Ewing sarcoma and other rare diseases when the available sample size is smaller than the guidance recommends?  Background  Clinical trials' data provides a rich resource to investigate secondary objectives, such as developing risk prediction (prognostic) models, which are needed to guide personalised treatment decisions. Such investigations often require larger sample sizes than those of the original trial. This is particularly problematic for clinical trials in rare diseases, where it can take a long time and international collaboration to recruit reasonable numbers. The PROGRESS framework recently published sample size formulae for prognostic model studies, providing the minimum sample size required to produce a stable model, with precise predictor effects [3]. However, in rare diseases, reaching the minimum sample size is highly unlikely and thus extensions to existing methods are required to facilitate their application.  Aims and objectives  The overarching aim of this PhD is to develop and examine statistical methods to overcome issues with small sample sizes in prognostic model research, with a specific application to Ewing sarcoma using the EE2012 clinical trial data (640 newly diagnosed Ewing sarcoma patients) [4].  The specific objectives are to:   Review literature to identify statistical methods for prognostic modelling in rare diseases,  Develop methods utilising Bayesian statistics,  Perform simulations studies to quantify the optimal method(s),  Develop a clinical risk prediction model for Ewing sarcoma patients,  Develop guidance to translate the prediction tool to clinical practice. Methods  A systematic review of the available methods to develop a prognostic model with small sample sizes will be performed. The best method(s) will then be examined through simulation studies. The results from these will inform the development of a clinical risk prediction model in Ewing sarcoma from the EE2012 trial data. Survival modelling methods will be utilised with event-free survival time (EFS) as the outcome. Model performance and internal validation methods (using bootstrapping) will be employed to assess the performance and stability of the model. Appropriate risk groups will be identified through meetings with PPI and collaborators to support clinical decision-making based on the patients' risk prediction.  Timelines for delivery  To date, a protocol for the development of a prognostic model from the EE2012 trial data has been written and will act as a benchmark model throughout my PhD. This model will be developed prior to the NIHR Doctoral Fellowship commencement. The anticipated timelines for my objectives are:              Objective            Timeline for completion (months)                  Systematic review            12                  Simulation studies            18                  Developing a clinical risk prediction model in Ewing sarcoma            12                  Translating risk from the model to clinical practice            9            Anticipated impact and dissemination  Guidance on statistical methods for prognostic modelling in rare diseases will be outlined. Upon application to Ewing sarcoma a clinical risk prediction model will be produced to inform treatment decisions based on individual risks, in consultation with patient and clinical user groups.  Clinical findings and statistical methodology will be published in high impact journals, presented at conferences and Ewing sarcoma specific meetings, and disseminated through social media.

title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) tool for measuring eczema severity in diverse skin tones
abstract: Research question Can eczema severity be reliably measured in a scalable way from digital images in people with diverse skin tones?    Background  Eczema is an itchy, chronic inflammatory skin condition that affects ~20% of UK children with a high socioeconomic burden. Timely and adequate treatment is critical to manage eczema symptoms to avoid worsening.   Teledermatology is fast becoming the norm. Eczema severity assessment is critical for deciding which treatments are needed and if specialist referral to secondary care is required. However, judging eczema severity on 2D images is challenging, especially for darker skin. Health care professionals need better support in remote assessment of eczema severity in diverse skin types to provide timely and appropriate treatment for people with eczema.  We have developed an artificial intelligence (AI) method that assesses eczema severity from digital images. The AI method works well on white skin but is less accurate for assessing darker skin tones, as the method was mainly developed using images of eczema on white skin.     Aim  To optimise an AI method (EczemaNet) so that it can be used as a medical device that robustly assesses eczema severity objectively from digital images for children and young people of diverse skin types.     Objectives & Methods    Establish regulatory-compliant design and development processes by developing Standard Operating Procedures.  Create a dataset of sufficient quality and representativeness of diverse skin types for the training of EczemaNet by collecting over 5,000 eczema images from ~500 paediatric patients of colour with clinician-diagnosed eczema. Collected images will be annotated with eczema severity scores assessed in-person by trained research nurses.  Train EczemaNet using augmented dataset of diverse skin tones, evaluate its effectiveness by cross-validation and develop regulatory-compliant Software as Medical Device.  Obtain qualitative feedback on the user experience of EczemaNet (acceptability, feasibility, and accessibility) from ~50 patients/carers and HCPs via structured interviews to inform future adoption into NHS practice  Update our existing business plan, including externally supplied analyses of Freedom-to-Operate, Health Care Economics and Regulatory Compliance and create technical files for CE marking.      Timelines for delivery This project will focus on bringing EczemaNet from a prototype to being fully ready for testing in clinical settings. Once completed, we will conduct a larger evaluation study (funded elsewhere) on the feasibility and reliability of EczemaNet in online clinical trials and an implementation project in different clinical settings.    Impacts and dissemination  EczemaNet will support telemedicine in NHS clinical and research practice, reducing the need for costly in-person assessments. It will provide an eczema-severity-scoring assist tool for GPs to match treatment to severity for people of diverse skin tones and facilitate the advice and guidance pathway between GPs and specialists, including when to refer them for specialist help.  Dissemination will be via social media, peer-reviewed journals, and presentations at national primary care and specialist meetings. Focused presentations will target key NHS Digital stakeholders, including NHS e-Referrals, clinical commissioning groups with teledermatology hubs, My Planned Care, and Wayfinder Integrated care systems.

title: Predictive RIsk Stratification Models: AssessmenT of Implementation Consequences (PRISMATIC 2)
abstract: We know that when patients are admitted to hospital as an emergency, they may stay in hospital for a long time and are at risk of losing mobility and independence. UK policy has supported initiatives to reduce emergency admissions, where possible. One widely implemented initiative in primary care has been the installation of software that predicts each patient's risk of emergency hospital admission. The software allocates a risk score to each patient that allows GPs to target management, such as medication review, to those at highest risk. This software has been introduced without knowing whether it brings benefits to patients or to the NHS. However, our evaluation of the introduction of predictive risk software in 32 general practices in the South Wales area (PRISMATIC trial) found that emergency admissions to hospital, Emergency Department (ED) attendances and days spent in hospital all increased when the software was available to GPs.  We propose to undertake PRISMATIC 2 to build on these findings to: 1. Assess effects of introducing emergency admission risk prediction software across England 2. Investigate whether GPs change how they manage risk and make decisions about admitting patients to hospital when the software is introduced 3. Understand patients' views about communication of risk scores by their GP   do they want to know if they are classified as high risk of emergency admission to hospital?  1. Using national data, we will look at changes in trends in emergency admission and other healthcare use that occurred when the software was made available. This approach is suited to this study with over 200 health commissioners - Clinical Commissioning Groups (CCGs) - across England and a range of dates when risk prediction software was implemented. We will look at anonymised data on emergency admissions, Emergency Department attendances and days spent in hospital in each CCG before and after the software was available so that we can understand whether there were any effects when it was introduced. 2. To understand why any changes might have happened, we will look more closely at the data in 16 GP practices in eight contrasting CCGs. We will explore whether GPs changed their decision making when the risk prediction software became available. For instance, did GPs lower their threshold for deciding to admit patients? Or did they prioritise patients in different ways once their risk scores were available to them? We will interview 48 members of staff including GPs at these practices to find out whether they think practice changed with implementation of the software. 3. We will carry out focus groups (x2) and interviews (x16) with patients to ask them whether they think hearing their own risk score may affect them, and if so, how.  PRISMATIC 2 will build on what we learnt in PRISMATIC and comprises the same core research team with its strong track record of research delivery. We have worked with patients and the public throughout this research programme. We will continue to involve PPI contributors in all aspects of research development, management, oversight, delivery and dissemination.  We will communicate findings to: * Patients to inform them about the use of risk prediction software and allow them to participate more fully in decisions about their own healthcare * NHS and social care staff and policy makers to ensure that the best evidence about the effects of risk prediction software can be used to inform practice and policy.

title: Development of AI Techniques to Predict Eye Cancer Using Big Longitudinal Data
abstract: Choroidal naevi are common pigmented fundus lesions (8% of the population) with a very low risk of conversion into choroidal melanoma. The increasing use of wide-angle fundus examinations by High Street Opticians and the fear of litigation if a melanoma is missed, has led to a rising number of referrals of pigmented fundus lesions to Ophthalmology and Ocular Oncology Units. This places a significant amount of pressure on Ophthalmology Departments in the country regarding new patient and follow-up appointments.  In order to address this clinical need, this project brings together an interdisciplinary team with distinct, complementary expertise in AI, medical image computing, and clinical medicine. The overarching aim is to develop and evaluate a novel, fully-automatic AI-powered diagnostic tool to support the accurate diagnosis and monitoring of choroidal naevi and to predict the risk of ocular melanoma. This research will harness (1) a unique database of ocular tumours, the largest of its kind worldwide, with a vast enriched dataset of images and clinical data of over 3000 patients, and (2) novel AI prognostic models that have been developed in Liverpool funded by EPSRC and NIHR.  Our specific objectives are: (1) to complete curation of a dataset essential for the development of AI tools, (2) to adopt a software development approach to develop and rigorously validate new AI tools by following TRIPOD and PROBAST principles and (3) to deliver the project by proactive managements, public engagement and risk mitigation and develop a robust commercialisation strategy to market. We expect by completion of the project to have developed AI tools ready for future prospective clinical study and commercialisation.  The project objective is well aligned with the NIHR AI funding strategy to advance translation of AI enabled healthcare technologies into new diagnostic tools to increase patient benefit and contribute economically to UK PLC.

title: Budget Impact Modelling of AI-assisted early fracture detection in the emergency department
abstract: X-ray is the first-line examination in the evaluation of bone trauma in emergency departments, but a lack of radiological resources restricts real-time interpretation by a trained expert, increasing the risk of errors. Fracture interpretation errors represent up to 80% of diagnostic errors in A&E (1), and up to 24% of harmful mis-diagnoses (2).   In the UK, between 2013-2018 the total cost of malpractice claims in radiology was £386.9m, with a significant amount due to missed fractures (3). Discordant interpretation of radiographic examinations occurs in up to 5.4%, but when the reporting is delayed this number increases to 7.9% (4,5,6). Only 8.7% of X-rays are reported before the patient s discharge (7), leading to inappropriate onward referrals to orthopaedic fracture clinics (8). Earlier accurate detection of normal XRs at the point of care could significantly reduce these associated costs.  Gleamer (France) has developed BoneView, an AI solution that detects fractures, dislocations and effusions on X-ray examinations and acts as an automated safety net. Its clinical relevance was demonstrated in two studies (9)(10), showing increased sensitivity, reduced reading time, and significant decrease in false positives and false negatives.   The lack of reimbursement pathways for AI technologies poses the question of financing. Financial pressure on hospitals prevents short-term investment without further evidence of direct return on investment.   Question: what is the 1-5 year direct budget impact for NHS Trusts to implement AI-assisted X-ray reporting for fractures? This will address the evidence gap of the ROI for trusts as a whole when implementing a technology that serves three departments: Accident & Emergency, Radiology and Orthopaedics.  This project will enable Trusts to understand the value proposition and budget impact, in keeping with the proposed NICE ESF, which highlights Budget Impact Modelling (BIM) as a key evidence requirement for novel health technologies.
