title: Improving specialist services for women who have experienced Female Genital Mutilation. A sequential mixed methods study to inform service transformation.
abstract: Background  Female Genital Mutilation (FGM) is when the female genitals are deliberately cut or injured without medical reason, carrying lifelong negative health consequences. Globally, more than 200 million women have suffered FGM, and this is a significant public health concern. An estimated 137,000 FGM survivors live in England and Wales, predominantly from Black Asian and Minority ethnic communities, costing the NHS approximately Â£100 million annually.  Early FGM specialist services adopted a biomedical approach to care, primarily aimed at pregnant women to ensure safe childbirth. Psychological support was rarely integrated into models of care. Where available, it was trauma-focused and often inaccessible to non-English speakers. Recently new clinics for non-pregnant women have been established, with co-located counsellors and health advocates. However, specialist provision varies considerably across the UK and no national standards exist for FGM care.  Women attending FGM clinics increasingly seek information about sexual function, bodily integrity, and reconstruction surgery but these topics rarely feature in UK-specific research. Surgery to restore original genital appearance does not exist in the UK but is available in other countries within holistic models integrating psychosexual assessment and therapies.  There is little evidence to underpin optimal FGM specialist care - service configuration, content of consultations, how women's needs are assessed, and what women and their partners want from services.    Research Question  Are specialist services for women who have experienced Female Genital Mutilation (and their partners) meeting their needs?   Aims  To: -  (1) map the configuration and content of FGM specialist services in the UK.  (2) explore women's and their partner's expectations and experiences of specialist care.  (3) identify information and treatment needs and make recommendations for theoretically-informed models of care.   Patient and Public Involvement  FGM survivors have said this research is important and will be involved throughout the study. Two PPI groups helped plan the project: -   FGM survivors.  Health Advocates (women from FGM-practising communities working in healthcare). A group for partners of FGM survivors will be established if funding is successful.   Project Plan  This is a sequential mixed method study.   Phase 1 - Identifying the evidence base. Undertake a comprehensive scoping review; Co-design questionnaires and topic guides with PPI members and expert advisory groups; Complete research protocol.      Phase 2 - Mapping FGM specialist service provision. Survey and documentary analysis of UK FGM clinics and three purposively sampled European clinics. Semi-structured interviews with lead clinicians to follow up questionnaire responses.         Phase 3 - Prospective Longitudinal study. Qualitative semi-structured interviews with 20 FGM survivors at two time points along the patient journey (within two weeks of initial appointment, and 3 months later); and interviews with 5 partners of FGM survivors.      Phase 4 - Data analysis and synthesis of findings to identify new information and treatment interventions and make recommendations for service configuration and provision.     Dissemination  Recommendations will be published in academic and practice-facing journals; shared through presentations, public events, social media, with study participants, policymakers and FGM specialists through professional networks. PPI members will co-design outputs and advise how findings are shared with FGM-practising communities.

title: The validation of an artificial intelligence model to generate automatic patient-centred summaries of GP consultations.
abstract: To enhance person-centred care, information about patients  clinical needs, their service encounters, and their own preferences should be shared across multidisciplinary teams (MDTs). Too often, this information is neither adequately recorded nor shared. Despite the limited time patients spend with their GPs(1) and the historic amounts of pressure the National Health Services (NHS) and GP practices are facing(2), important conversations are happening with GPs every day, which alone have been reported to be healing(3). Artificial intelligence (AI) models that automatically summarise these encounters can help alleviate his pressure. Unfortunately, existing models were developed to mimic current summarization practices of doctors that focus more on clinical needs or issues and less on patients  preferences, values, and concerns(4). The aim of this project is to test if our AI model can overcome this limitation and develop person-centred post-encounter summaries.  We have developed a more explainable AI-model that automatically generates summaries from multiple documents or dialogues(5). Our model was developed by using large language models (i.e. LongT5) and it was validated on 165,000 set of webpages and 3,673 transcripts of dialogues from TV episodes. The difference between this model and other summarization models (e.g. GPT-4) is that our model has an intermediate planning step that allows us to explain and personalize the automatic summarization process. However, our model has not yet been validated on clinical settings.  Our proposal, which aligns with the FAST priority of AI for primary care settings, is to test and validate our AI summarization model on the generation of person-centred summaries of patients-GPs clinical encounters in real-life scenarios. To test if these summaries are person-centred clinical summaries, we will use Patient and Public Involvement (PPI) groups throughout our study.

title: Explainable machine learning models for clinical decision support in kidney transplant offering
abstract: Background The disparity between the size of the waiting list and the availability of donor kidneys means that clinicians often consider organs from suboptimal donors for transplantation. Such decisions can be challenging, and no decision support tools are currently available to help support clinicians and patients. Aims and objectives We aim to create a clinical decision support tool that will help a clinician and patient make a personalised decision about a given organ offer. This phase 1 project will train and validate machine learning (ML) models that accurately predict both graft and patient survival if a transplant goes ahead, as well as the outcome if the offer is declined and the patient waits for a subsequent offer. We will also undertake initial scoping work with patients and clinicians to determine the best way to present these predictions to patients and clinicians at the point of organ offer. Subsequent phases will develop the clinical decision tool based on these models and evaluate its use in clinical trials. Methods We will use data from the UK transplant registry to train ML models that predict post-transplant graft and patient survival, as well as patient outcomes if the offer is declined. These models will be validated in independent subsets of the data to assess performance and compared to existing regression-based approaches. We will undertake semi-structured interviews to explore optimum methods of data presentation in the proposed clinical decision tool. Timelines Phase 1 will take 12 months, with model development and user requirement scoping running in parallel. Impact and dissemination Development of a clinical decision aid will help to reduce disparity in decision making, improve informed consent and potentially improve organ utilisation. Results of the study will be disseminated via peer-reviewed journals, conferences and transplant organisations, and communicated in plain English to patient groups.

title: JoyConnect - an AI assistant that helps GPs address the Wider Determinants of Health for their patients
abstract: Research suggests that more than half of the major causes of mortality and morbidity in the UK come from preventable diseases, linked to people s behaviours and the social determinants of health1. 20% of GPs  time is spent discussing these preventable issues, rather than on the immediate medical conditions they re trained to address1.  Often GPs feel ill-equipped to effectively connect patients to support services, and more could be done to streamline care navigation and ensure patients have access to the support they need2.  We are proud to introduce  JoyConnect : a cutting-edge, integrative AI platform designed to increase successful patient referrals to social and community-based treatment pathways. JoyConnect - a small desktop  widget  - operates as an AI assistant during GP consultations. Utilising postcode searches and information stored on a patient s medical record, JoyConnect notifies clinicians of suggested local support services that might benefit a patient s health. It ambitiously seeks to reduce average waiting times, limit the encumbrance on frontline staff3, and holistically improve patient outcomes.  The Joy system4 is already successfully used by Social Prescribing Linked Workers across 1,200 GP surgeries, covering 13 million patients nationwide. It has established interoperability with EMIS and SystmOne, contains a database of 10,000 local services for the wider determinants of health, and successfully refers 4,000 patients every week.  We seek funding to further develop the AI capabilities of JoyConnect and make it accessible to GP staff rather than just Social Prescribing Link Workers.  The development of the initial Joy system was co-designed with a patient advisory group (N=30) who participated in focus groups and surveys surrounding referral to non-clinical support. This continuous PPI is integral in ensuring any Joy innovation is collaborative and directly aligned with patients  needs.

title: Evaluating the health economic impact of an AI-powered cardiac diagnostic tool
abstract: Powerful Medical's innovative product, PMcardio, represents a significant advancement in cardiac diagnostics, utilising AI and deep neural networks. Developed using a vast dataset of 12-lead electrocardiograms (ECGs) from 172,000 patients, PMcardio underwent a rigorous evaluation with an independent testing dataset containing 11,900 annotated ECG labels.  What truly distinguishes PMcardio is its ability to outperform GPs and even cardiologists in all five evaluated categories, due to its combination of AI, advanced algorithms, and statistical modeling. PMcardio has exhibited non-inferiority to cardiologists, a remarkable achievement in cardiology.  The standard 12-lead ECG allows for a rapid assessment of cardiac abnormalities. ECG interpretation requires considerable expertise and training, with studies showing that physicians at all training levels have deficiencies in ECG interpretation, and request support, even after educational interventions. Accurate ECG interpretation has been measured at 54% across all healthcare professional training levels, with non-cardiologist practicing physicians achieving 68.5% [1].  Traditional computerized interpretation of electrocardiograms (CIE) has limitations, with reported accuracy rates as low as 54% for non-sinus rhythms and error rates of 40.7% and 75.0% for diagnosing acute coronary syndrome or higher degree AV block, respectively [2-4]. Physicians are advised against relying on CIE to drive clinical decision-making [5], with interpretation often significantly influenced by CIE and errors overlooked [6-9].  PMcardio addresses these shortcomings, excelling in identifying acute cardiac conditions, including subtle changes in ECG readings that manual analysis might miss. Notably, it stands out in identifying occlusion myocardial infarctions without clear ST-segment elevations. Unlike personal monitoring devices, more suitable for detecting arrhythmias and long-term heart conditions, PMcardio plays a crucial role in the early detection and immediate treatment of life-threatening conditions such as heart attacks.  PMcardio's clinical performance has been proven in peer-reviewed publications, demonstrating efficacy and ability to provide more definitive and comprehensive results, empowering clinicians with more accurate information.

title: CESCAIL - Capsule Endoscopy delivery at SCale through enhanced AI anaLysis
abstract: Bowel cancer is a key target for innovation in early detection and diagnosis. Here, we propose coupling a minimally-invasive imaging device with Artificial Intelligence to improve efficiency and accuracy of an investigation. Colon capsule endoscopy (CCE) is a clinically viable and cost-effective alternative to traditional imaging methods of the gastrointestinal tract. CCE provides several benefits to patients, clinicians, and the healthcare system, including adding urgently needed capacity to markedly strained services. Analysing CCE videos, however, is resource intensive, represents a time-consuming workload for clinicians, and slows the roll-out of CCE due to staffing constraints. AI can mitigate these constraints, as shown successfully in an Innovate UK-funded project, where a machine learning algorithm has been developed to create a tool ('AiSPEED') that supports the pre-processing of CCE videos to detect polyps. An expert achieves better accuracy in less than 20% of time. To conduct clinical validation, the AI algorithm will be locked and in a clinical trial accuracy for polyp detection as well as time spent compared against the 'gold standard' standard care pathway (months 4-16). Results will then support certification (months 1-13) Governed by a predetermined change control plan and using trial data, AiSPEED's accuracy will be improved by using image sequences for machine learning, mimicking the human expert approach (months 2-15) rendering able to classify more pathology categories (months 10-13). The primary objective of this project will be a highly efficient Software-as-Medical-Device, ready for MDR Class IIa certification and acceptance into the standard care pathway. title: How can we help NHS England integrate the United Nations AI for Good system for national deployment of the Body Volume Index (BVI) obesity solution?
abstract: In August 2022, Select Scanning Ltd received a 100% funded Innovate UK grant for  “The Body Volume Index (BVI) - Deployment of obesity solution for the NHS and WHO”. This successful project has now led to an unmet health need to embed ethical AI for delivery and execution of BVI as a new valid digital obesity and health risk measurement.   In terms of patient or public involvement conducted to date and how this will inform the development of the innovation, this has been undertaken by WMAHSN (now HIWM), reviewed by the NHS Innovation Service, and supported by NICE. Extensive patient and NHS practitioner feedback was provided for this comprehensive review, managed by Wessex AHSN.   Our project aligns with the scope of the call to apply artificial intelligence data to primary care settings because we have now secured commitment from the United Nations AI for Good Program to allow integration of their ethical AI platform for the NHS. Tackling obesity and health risk also complies with the UN Sustainable Development Goals.   BVI is fully developed to Technology Readiness Level 8 (TRL8) and at present, high-level discussions between the Department of Health and the United Nations AI for Good about the integration of this system are occurring. It is possible that an agreement may be forthcoming for the UN AI for Good system to become integrated into the NHS in Autumn 2024.  This integration will be further explored in this project for Select Scanning effectively to act as a broker to help integrate the AI for Good system for the NHS. This is based upon the experience we have of liaising with WHO about UN AI for Good, another consequence of the 2022 Innovate UK funding.

title: AI-supported colorectal polyp detection (DAP78)
abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC), also known as bowel cancer, includes cancer of the colon or rectum (1). It is the fourth most common cancer in the UK, with over 44,000 new cases each year, and accounts for 10% of all cancer-related deaths in the UK. It is the second most common cause of cancer-related death; the earlier it can be diagnosed, the better the chances of survival (2-4).  Colorectal polyps are small growths on the lining of the colon or rectum that are usually asymptomatic but may be detected on colonoscopy. Symptoms such as rectal bleeding or a change in bowel habits can occur in some cases. Most colorectal polyps are harmless, but some have the potential to turn into cancer over time if untreated (5). Colonoscopy is the gold standard for the detection of colorectal polyps. People may undergo colonoscopy through various pathways, as summarised in Figure 1. Overview of groups offered colonoscopy (reproduced from NICE DAP78 scope)   During a colonoscopy, concerning polyps can be removed. In the UK, all removed polyps are sent for histopathological testing to classify them as neoplastic or non-neoplastic. Neoplastic polyps, such as adenomas and serrated polyps, have a higher risk of developing into cancer. Some polyps may need to be removed during a separate procedure, and endoscopists may choose not to remove certain polyps if they are confident they are not neoplastic. A  resect and discard  strategy, where an optical diagnosis by the endoscopist would suffice without histopathological testing, is in its early stages of use within the Bowel Cancer Screening Programme (BCSP).  In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI)-supported colonoscopy technologies have been developed. These include computer-aided detection (CADe) and computer-aided diagnosis (CADx). CADe aims to reduce missed polyps by flagging areas of interest to for review, while CADx involves characterising detected polyps to suggest whether they are likely neoplastic, supporting decisions about resection. This may reduce resections of non-neoplastic polyps and increase neoplastic polyp resection.  This assessment will review the evidence for the clinical and cost-effectiveness of specific AI-supported colonoscopy technologies, including CADe and CADx. The systematic literature review (SLR) will aim to identify evidence related to clinical effectiveness, diagnostic accuracy, safety and other outcomes. Previous economic evaluations will be reviewed, and a new economic model may be developed to assess whether the technologies represent a good use of NHS resources, where sufficient data are available. title: Development and Validation of a contactless tool for measuring patient tremor
abstract: Background  Tremor affects one million people in the UK and is a common manifestation of many neurological diseases, drug side effects, and psychological disorders. It is usually assessed via human judgement. However, assessment is time consuming and can differ between assessors. An accelerometer can be used to provide objective measures of tremor severity, but few hospitals have access to this equipment.  Our aim is to develop and validate software that accurately measures tremor frequency and amplitude using only smartphone or webcam video. In previous work, we have already demonstrated how tremor frequency can be ascertained from smartphone videos. Therefore, the scientific objectives of the project are (i) to develop and validate a method to measure tremor amplitude from video (ii) to validate the resulting tremor frequency and amplitude software (iii) to assess usability of the software (iv) to conduct exploratory data analysis using deep learning to classify clinical tremor type.  Methods  Objective (i) - To develop contactless tremor amplitude measurement, we need to accurately assess object depth. We will investigate three approaches: parallax depth estimation, LIDAR sensor, and Densedepth neural network. We will collect pilot data from healthy volunteers, mimicking tremor, to refine our data collection process. We will then collect patient hand tremor videos (N=60), recorded on smartphone and webcam. Approaches will be compared to an objective standard using Bland-Altman analysis to provide 95% limits of agreement for tremor amplitude.  The best performing approach will be used, alongside our previous tremor frequency algorithm, to develop standalone software for smartphone camera and webcam.  Objective (ii) - We will collect further tremor videos from patients to assess the software. Amplitude will be assessed as in Objective (i). Frequency will be compared to clinical-grade accelerometer, using a Bland-Altman analysis.  Objective (iii) – We will assess usability via a time-motion study of clinical users of the software. This will be supported by qualitative user surveys and interviews.  Objective (iv) - In secondary exploratory analysis, we will apply 3D convolutional neural networks to the videos collected for (ii) to determine whether subtle clinical features can be extracted from the raw video to automatically distinguish between different types of clinical tremor. We will report cross-validation F1-score, sensitivity and specificity.  Delivery Timeline  All objectives will be completed within 24 months. Objective (i) is scheduled for M1-M9, Objective (ii) is scheduled for M8 to M18, Objective (iii) is scheduled for M13 to M18, and Objective (iv) is scheduled for M18 to M24.  Impact and dissemination  This project will deliver a clinically validated tool to quantify hand tremor frequency and amplitude. We expect it to have high translational impact amongst doctors and other clinicians, especially neurologists, GPs, geriatricians, and researchers. Results describing the development of methods, development of software, and validation of software, will be written for publication in high-impact clinical and health informatics journals. Finally, the work will provide a platform for us to conduct larger-scale research into digital biomarkers, by providing an infrastructure for research video data to be collected and securely stored from multiple sites.

title: Establishing natural language processing (NLP) functionality for clinical term extraction within a rare disease case-finding tool stack.
abstract: There are over 7,000 Rare Diseases (RDs), affecting 1 in 17 people. RD diagnostic journeys are long and fraught with misdiagnoses and healthcare resource inefficiencies (Diagnostic Odyssey).(1)  We have a suite of digital clinical decision support tools that expedite the diagnosis of hard-to-diagnose RDs and ensure timely access to appropriate management. MendelScan, a MHRA-registered Medical Device, is used for RD case-finding within various NHS primary care settings.(2)  All our tools currently depend solely on the structured data in electronic health records (EHRs). Structured data contains valuable summary information, yet it is known to be incomplete and lacks context. Utilising only this aspect of the EHRs limits the number of cases identified and reduces efficiency (within our tools and in the downstream clinical reviews).   We aim to build a natural language processing (NLP) prototype tool which will extract useful information from the unstructured clinical text within EHRs (referral letters, discharge summaries, clinical notes, test reports etc.).  Clinically-validated and regulation-compliant NLP and clinically-relevant generative large language model AI tools are now routinely available from a number of technology providers globally (incl. Google, Amazon Web Services (AWS), OpenAI and Stability AI as Software as a Service (SaaS) tools.(3,4,5,6) We have successfully run a number of internal proof of concept trials extracting clinical terms from clinical case notes.  The addition of a NLP tool, either as a standalone, or a major and non-incremental addition to MendelScan, is expected to significantly increase our ability to accurately and efficiently identify patients for further diagnostic workup or stratification.  Our PPI board confirms the acceptance and desire for EHR data to be utilised for the sake of patient health in such a way. This is a sentiment that is strongly echoed in various PPI studies(7) including a survey we currently have open to the public.

title: Transforming Outcomes for Paediatric allergy in primary care (TOPIC)
abstract: Children commonly develop one or more long-term atopic conditions: eczema, food allergy, asthma or allergic rhinitis. Food allergy is more common in children with eczema. Symptoms and burden of management of both conditions have a big impact on those affected. The social and financial costs to children, parents and the health service are also significant. Most children can and have to be managed by their GP, because access to NHS specialist dermatology and allergy services is poor. The relationship between, and research into, eczema and food allergy is complex and challenging.   Research is needed on how to best use existing eczema treatments and structure patient's care. We know that parents have concerns about the core treatments for eczema (emollients and topical corticosteroids - TCS) and support in primary care for parents to self-manage the condition is suboptimal. Labelling parents as 'non-adherent' and 'steroid phobic' is unhelpful because emollients and TCS can both cause harms and there is limited research on how best to use them together, effectively and safely. Eczema care, like asthma, may benefit from a greater emphasis on topical corticosteroids and regular review in dedicated clinics.   Food allergy is complex and there is a primary care-relevant evidence void. Research to date has focused on immunology and is commercially influenced. Patient and clinician priorities for food allergy research need to be established. The most relevant, recent research supports early introduction of allergens to prevent food allergy, especially peanut and egg in children with eczema. However, the uptake and impact of changes in complementary feeding (weaning) advice, some of which is conflicting, is uncertain.   The aim of this professorship is to transform the treatment of eczema, and research into food allergy and its prevention, in children. Over five work packages, I will lead research that will:     a) Through a systematic review, surveys and interviews improve understanding of real world use of topical treatments; and b) Co-design a trial of how best to use emollients and TCS in combination  a) Develop a primary care eczema clinic; and b) evaluate it in a cluster trial  a) Determine the research priorities of parents and clinicians for food allergy in children, and b) deliver at least one study addressing at least one of the identified research priorities  Through surveys, interviews and a cohort study assess understanding, implementation and effects of early allergen introduction advice  Integrate public, patient (parent/child) and stakeholder opinion into all of the above, ensuring inclusivity and relevance of the research to all of society   The programme of work is ambitious, striking a balance between building on existing work, with guaranteed deliverables within five years (1a,2a&b,3a,4&5), and more open-ended projects (1b&3b) which promise a step-change in trajectory with high impact in five years.   Close working with patient public partners and stakeholders, paying attention to inclusivity, spans all the above programme of work. They will help plan, and assist with, the dissemination of findings, using a range of approaches tailored to the target audiences.

title: The development of a novel model of undergraduate General Practice clinical placement to increase placement capacity: a study using implementation science and co-production
abstract: Background There have been calls for undergraduate medical student teaching to become more community-focussed (1, 2). Targets have been set for 25% of undergraduate clinical teaching to be delivered in (GP) (3, 4): a significant increase, with current provision at 9.2%(5). Placement capacity in GP is a serious challenge for many medical schools (6), driven by a shortage of GPs and other clinical pressures within primary care (7).  Clinical placement design plays a key role in influencing placement capacity (8). The traditional model of GP clinical placement in the UK, the 'apprenticeship model', involves one or two students attached to a practice, supervised by a GP. It is heavily GP-led and costly in time and resources (3). However, alternative models of clinical placement have been developed which may build placement capacity (8, 9). Examples include collaborative, and hub and spoke, models. These developments originate pre-dominantly from nursing, and rural medical, placements. There is an opportunity to build on existing evidence of promising clinical placement models, and to develop these for implementation into a GP, undergraduate context.  Aim  To develop, and pilot, a novel, evidence-based model of undergraduate GP clinical placement capable of increasing GP teaching capacity; and to understand its wider benefits for medical students and key stakeholders, in relation to local and national health professions education priorities.  Objectives   To synthesise evidence from the medical and allied healthcare professions literature on clinical placement models capable of increasing placement capacity.  To understand the barriers and facilitators to implementation of these different placement approaches into a GP, undergraduate context.  To use co-production methods, empirical evidence, and implementation science, to develop and pilot a placement model capable of increasing GP undergraduate teaching capacity; and to understand the wider benefits to students and stakeholders. title: Precision Treatment Strategies in Multiple Sclerosis Using Next-generation Machine Learning
abstract: Research question How can data-driven multiple sclerosis (MS) types be matched with specific treatment strategies in real-world settings to improve patient outcomes?   Background  Currently, we have more than 15 MS treatments with different risk profiles. There is a discrepancy between MS types and underlying disease mechanisms. Therefore, treatments selected based on MS type may be ineffective, as they imprecisely target disease mechanisms. I have recently developed a data-driven model to classify MS types with brain MRI to address this discrepancy in clinical trials. However, clinical trials do not represent the diversity of patients seen in routine care. I now want to develop novel models for the real world to enable widespread patient benefit.   Aims, objectives and methods  I aim to define biologically-driven MS types and match them with effective treatment strategies in real-world settings. This will enable us to (1) recommend the right treatments according to the likely treatment response and (2) enrol patients from real-world registries with specific disease biology into precision medicine studies to develop new treatments.  I will use unique existing data sets from the UK (seven NHS Trusts) and two international collaborators (Montreal Neurological Institute, Canada and MS Center Amsterdam, the Netherlands). I will build novel machine learning models to:  (Objective 1) Classify MS into MRI- and serum-derived types. I will combine MRI information with serum neurofilament light-chain (sNfL), an emerging biomarker for future use in clinical practice. This information will be combined with clinical data to stratify patients for the risk of disability, which can then be matched with treatment effects.  (Objective 2) Predict individualised treatment effect. Unlike clinical trials, evaluating treatment effects is challenging in the real world. To assess and predict treatment effects, I will develop causal machine learning models to generate individualised 'simulated' outcomes to answer the question: How would a patient's outcome be different if they received a specific treatment? These models will perform individual-level predictions conditioned on a set of baseline characteristics. This will also improve predictions of treatment effects from data-driven types in objective (1).  (Objective 3) Scale up models for future deployment in the NHS. Within objectives (1) and (2), I will build privacy-preserving models to learn from diverse MS populations at different centres without sharing patients' data. Across different centres, to make personalised solutions possible, I will also evaluate the effects of comorbidities, gender, age group and ethnicity on model performance. I will quantify the healthcare cost savings that a future diagnostic decision support system may bring by enabling earlier treatments and reducing adverse events.   Timelines for delivery  Over five years, my fellowship will output research tools for (1) disease classification and risk-stratification models; (2) software to enrol MS patients from real-world routine care for precision medicine studies; and (3) privacy-preserving machine learning models.   Anticipated impact and dissemination  My fellowship will provide essential tools for future diagnostic decision support systems to choose the best treatment for patients and delay disability. I will disseminate outcomes through scientific publications, congresses, lay language summaries and Q&A video recordings.

title: Robotics and AI platform for minimally invasive Neurosurgery (RAIN)
abstract: Introduction Endonasal surgery, one of the best examples of endoscopic neurosurgery, allows skull-base tumour removal through the natural orifice of the nostril. Although a promising alternative to invasive transcranial approaches, it comes with its limitations, mainly the lack of instrument articulation within the constrained operative spaces. The same practical constraints apply to many other procedures such as Endoscopic Sinus Surgery, Endoscopic Ventriculostomy and Endoscopic Spine Surgery. Thus, surgical innovation is needed since these surgeries are limited to specialised centres, reducing patient access and straining hospitals with high referral costs and readmission rates. We are proposing an innovative solution, the Robotics and AI platform for minimally invasive Neurosurgery (RAIN), which deploys handheld robotic instruments to increase the surgeon s dexterity, and AI-assistance software to support their decision-making. Our platform can make endoscopic neurosurgery safer, more effective, and feasible in more clinical cases.  Methods Currently, our RAIN platform consists of a core-set of robotic instruments with flexible tips and preliminary AI-assistance software around surgical-phase recognition and anatomy segmentation. With this project, we aim to expand our instruments portfolio to include specialised articulated instruments incorporating vision, suction and energy. Simultaneously, we will further develop our machine-learning algorithms, to produce a fully-integrated platform. The RAIN platform will be evaluated for its safety and feasibility during an IDEAL Stage 1 first-in-human study, comprising six patients with skull-base tumours.  Timelines for delivery Due to its instinctive handheld control and affordable cost, the RAIN platform has the potential to be quickly adopted by neurosurgeons. A two-year plan dictates the activities of this project. Within the first 16 months, we will develop our instrument portfolio and machine-learning software, and spend the remaining time for integration into a single RAIN platform. To conduct our first-in-human study, MHRA regulatory approval for use of a non-certified device will be acquired within 19 months, allowing 5 months for delivery. This feasibility study will generate clinical data to support subsequent fundraising, and wider studies that will lead to multi-region certification within the next 2 years after the project ends.  Dissemination Patients involvement has been pivotal since the inception of our technology suggesting the use of handheld robotics and playing an active role in shaping this proposal. Moreover, a patient advisory group will be consulted throughout this project. Thus, we understand the importance of disseminating our project outputs to patients, the scientific community and to the general public. We intend to do so via short videos, infographics, events, and peer-reviewed journal articles.  Discussion In this project, a Robotics and AI platform for minimally invasive Neurosurgery will be developed and evaluated during a first-in-human clinical study. Our disruptive solution can democratise endoscopic neurosurgery by enhancing it with the benefits of robotic surgery, only at a fraction of its cost. This will allow more surgeons to perform keyhole procedures expanding the number of patients that can enjoy their benefits and cutting down referral costs. Additionally, the occurrence of repeat-procedures due to complications or incomplete tumour resection will be reduced, freeing up hospital beds and resources.

title: Assess the feasibility of an AI-enhanced Urology Triage Platform ( AI-UTP) to augment clinical capabilities of front line Junior Medical and Allied Healthcare Professional staff
abstract: Urology referrals to secondary care have risen by nearly 20% over the last 20 years and now account for 5% of all outpatient appointments (2.2m appointments annually[1]) with patient demand expected to rapidly increase, largely linked to our ageing population.   This is creating considerable NHS and patient burden. The NHS spends >£650m in Urology secondary care referrals. Patients being referred for non-2WW (two week wait) urology services now face 18-week+ waits for a first outpatient appointment in most trusts, leading to negative patient impacts and operational pressures on primary and secondary care services[2]. At Guys and St Thomas  (GSTT) our urology team face these challenges head-on, whilst acting as a centre of excellence.  The Urology Guidance Outpatients Transformation has identified the importance of improved primary care referrals, greater support of specialists advice for primary care assessment and a greater emphasis on MDT clinical resources including specialist nurses to play a greater role in increasing the capacity of Urology assessment services.  A study estimated that ~50% of urology referrals from primary care were unnecessary, and could have been improved with greater awareness of urology guidelines and specialist support in their clinical assessment[3].  DemDx, an innovative health technology company, has an existing AI enhanced Ophthalmology Triage Platform co-developed with Moorfield Eye Hospital NHS Trust focused on improving the quality of ophthalmology referrals into secondary from primary care, with data demonstrating 5% (3.2%-6.7%) reduction in urgent referrals[4].   GSTT Urology team will collaborate with DemDx to translate and refine the existing AI algorithms to the Urology speciality, adding a focus on junior medical and allied health professional triaging patterns, with the intention of demonstrating the clinical safety and technical suitability of the AI within the speciality. This will unlock the roadmap to creating a Urology Triage Platform (UTP) realising significant and urgently needed efficiencies.

title: SEISMIC SHIFT: Systemic Health Innovation Future Transformation
abstract: It is widely accepted that the NHS as the UK's healthcare system cannot continue on its current trajectory. Public opinion, political will and media focus have combined to exert pressure on a system that cannot sustain many of its existing ways to deliver its services. It is clearly time to effect a radical change in the way the NHS interacts with its service users whether they are patients, carers, the healthy well or other stakeholders. This proposed project takes a systems approach to find out how feasible and acceptable such changes would be. We see an increase in demand on health care service provision caused by an ageing population, whether in overburdened urban centres or in difficult to reach remote and rural settlements. Multimorbidity is increasingly prevalent, starting in early adulthood and midlife, leading to an increasing risk of chronic diseases for older people, and impacting patient quality of life and carer burden. Patients with long term conditions who often suffer from multimorbidity and who may also have complex care needs face physical, psychological, and practical challenges that can be exacerbated by current patterns of health service delivery which have distinct, ie non-integrated approaches to patient care. In other words, service users can end up with multiple health service interactions across a number of disease silos, meaning multiple hospital visits to outpatients, contacts, or other such demands. Pressure on the NHS is increased by demands on staff, partly caused by staff shortages and partly by the type and volume of these demands.   The challenge posed by all of these demands and pressures is systemic and pervasive. One of the key issues is that health service delivery is organised largely based on disease-specialisms, i.e. cardiologists treat patients for heart disease while lung diseases are seen by respiratory specialists. This is not reflecting the lived experience of the conditions together as a whole and it is also not managing the patient or service delivery holistically. A radical change would be to reverse this traditional disease focussed approach and instead deliver services with symptoms as the instigator of management, including prevention, diagnosis, treatment and long-term management. Looking at the whole-person in an integrated manner would be a paradigm-shift, and this is at the heart of the proposal. SEISMIC SHIFT is a consortium of design and engineering researchers, clinical researchers, and improvement specialists from NHS Lanarkshire and NHS Highland who are focussing increasingly on modelling and understanding such interdependencies. During this development phase to the Innovation Hub, pilot examples will be used to demonstrate the new focus on symptoms. This will allow identification of leverage points that can support change within the healthcare system to desirable to-be states. Breathlessness as a core symptom in respiratory care will form one example with associated co-morbidities, acknowledging health inequalities and differences across rural and urban geographies. Another example will take breathlessness as a core symptom of heart failure with associated co-morbidities. These two clinical specialisms are clearly linked but to-date generally treated within each specialism. In the Hub, we will together work to achieve integrated care and ultimately prevention by focusing on modifiable risk factors, health promotion, and an overall salutogenic vision of health and care provision.

title: Co-creation of training resources for AI-powered N-Tidal - tackling a key barrier to adoption
abstract: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) is a progressive incurable respiratory disease, usually associated with tobacco smoking. Over 1.4 million people have COPD in the UK, with at least 0.4 million undiagnosed [1] resulting in £3.9 billion of direct costs in England. [2]  Over 22% of people wait over five years for a diagnostic test for COPD after noticing symptoms. [3]  Part of this cost is due to the poor availability and imprecision of spirometry, the current diagnostic test. There is a need for a low cost, simple, fast and accurate test for COPD that could be delivered in primary care. [4-5]  TidalSense has developed the N-Tidal Screen (NTS), a Class 1 UKCA marked device, with extensive patient and clinical input into prototype design and testing, formal usability assessment and potential pathway integration. It is an easy to use handheld device that measures carbon dioxide (CO2) during normal breathing and then applies artificial intelligence (AI) derived diagnostic algorithms to accurately output a probability of COPD. [6] The test takes 5 minutes to administer and requires no formal accreditation, meaning the time and human resources required are significantly less compared to spirometry, making primary care an optimal place to deliver the test.  NTS has been released to facilitate early deployment and real-world testing (such as this project). The definitive diagnostic release will be N-Tidal Diagnose (NTD), a Class 2 EU MDR medical device with expected certificate of conformity in mid-2024. NTD has attracted significant commercial interest with expected rollout across primary care in Suffolk and North East Essex Integrated Care Board from mid-2024. Real-world feedback has established that those interpreting the novel AI-driven results of NTS and NTD are less familiar with the output than existing technology and would benefit from training to improve their confidence in implementation of the result.

title: Assessing an AI enabled solution for Lung Cancer Screening using the Digital Technology Assessment Criteria (DTAC)
abstract: Unmet-Need -Lung cancer is one of the most common cancers in the UK. title: Optimising Patient Outcomes: AI-Driven Identification of Effective Treatment Components for Depression and Anxiety in Long-Term and Multimorbid Illnesses in Primary Care.
abstract: The unmet health need is the lack of recognition and treatment of emotional distress in individuals with long-term conditions (LTC), often overlooked in the healthcare system's disease-centric approach (1). Neglecting mental health results in worsened symptoms, with 50% of GP appointments dedicated to LTC (2). Enhanced mental health correlates with better self-management, potentially reducing the 70%  spend in health and social care. Despite the proven impact of self-care, 45% of LTC individuals lack confidence in self-management (3) .  Our innovation will address depression/anxiety in  LTC,  with AI informed self-management - AI insights predicting optimal treatments in individuals and disease clusters. This aligns with the FAST call, leveraging AI in primary care to enhance the management of long-term illnesses, including multimorbidity.   This innovation builds on the existing NHS DTAC-accredited, resilience, audio, Feeling Good app (FGA) to create a cutting-edge AI-driven platform to specifically improve LTC patient outcomes. Proof of concept (TRL 3) comes from studies of the  FGA, a supervised, self-help, tier C Digital Health Technology, developed and used in primary care, with proven efficacy in peer-reviewed publications in treating depression/anxiety (4, 5, 6),  increasing self-confidence and autonomy (7), internal audit and report (8).   Our AI-driven innovation addresses the evidence gap by collecting and analysing anxious/depressed LTC patient's experiences; identifying the most beneficial treatment options;  tailoring unique recommendations for faster, more effective outcomes;  improving patient symptoms related to anxiety/depression, sleep, and treatment adherence;  decreasing patient demands on primary care services.  Patient involvement is central.  PPI activities to date include  interview s, questionnaires, and an in-depth study with stroke survivors (9). The grant will enable an extended PPI advisory group of patients, carers, and clinicians, evaluating question acceptability; providing feedback on prototype design and use. They will be drawn from our existing NHS primary care user base in Lothian, Kent, and Northampton.

title: ANNA: Revolutionising Early Diagnosis of Endometriosis with Artificial Intelligence (AI)-powered Consultations in Primary Care
abstract: Endometriosis, affecting about 10% of UK women, faces diagnostic challenges and often goes unnoticed early on.[1-4]  Patients typically wait 7-9 years for a diagnosis, leading to decreased quality of life and health outcomes due to delays in specialist consultations and surgeries.[5-8]  MetaDoc s response to this issue is ANNA (Artificial Narrow Neural Assistant),[9] an AI-driven web application designed to facilitate real-time consultations and support early diagnosis of endometriosis. ANNA employs Autoregressive Large Language Model Neural Network (LLMNN) algorithms, based on 283,000 publications and 47,000 clinical algorithms. Overseen by a committee from the UK Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RCOG), ANNA ensures up-to-date clinical accuracy. Its user-friendly interface, supporting 63 languages through text, voice messages, and a culturally sensitive avatar, addresses common issues like language barriers and outdated training data found in other AI products.[10]  ANNA can be used on multiple devices. It analyses symptoms and asks specific questions, providing insights and advice to hasten the endometriosis diagnosis. ANNA is a critical tool in primary care, assisting patients and healthcare professionals in triage and diagnosis, potentially shortening the treatment initiation time. For patients, ANNA suggests appropriate times for seeking specialist or GP consultations and offers pain management advice. For healthcare professionals, it bolsters diagnostic accuracy, enhances disease understanding, and provides multilingual support.[11-15]  ANNA is a NICE Tier 3 digital technology as it directly impacts health outcomes and informs clinical management and diagnosis. Currently, at the proof-of-concept stage, it has shown 100% agreement with specialist advice in a 10-month study of 160 patients in UK endometriosis clinics.[16,17] However, further refinements are necessary for its application in primary care.  PPIE-ANNA s development has been enriched by qualitative feedback from 160 gynaecological outpatients. Three patient representatives reviewed the application and will be involved in WP1,WP2,WP3. Ten people with endometriosis will be consulted in WP2.

title: POCUS4TB: NIHR Global Health Group on AI-assisted point-of-care ultrasound (AI-POCUS) for TB screening
abstract: This research aims to develop a simple, cheap imaging solution to screen for  tuberculosis (TB), the world's leading infectious disease killer. The World Health Organisation has set a target to "End TB  by 2035, and developed a strategy to help countries achieve this. One of the key activities in this strategy is to find and treat more people with TB. Current screening guidelines include chest x-ray, but this is inaccessible to many of the poorest people worldwide who are most at need of screening for TB. Ultrasound may provide a solution. Ultrasound is a simple and safe procedure that can be used for adults and children. Portable ultrasound probes ( Point-of-care  ultrasound, POCUS) that can connect to mobile phones are available and could be placed at the lowest levels of the health care system in countries most affected by TB. Initial research is promising, but highly trained health workers able to interpret ultrasound images are not widely available. Therefore, artificial intelligence (AI) could provide a solution. This Global Health Research Group (GHRG) will bring together researchers from four high TB burden countries; Mozambique, Zambia, Bolivia and Peru , alongside a medical imaging partner to  develop an AI-supported POCUS tool. The first activity of the GHRG will be to host a workshop inviting researchers from around the world who have any expertise in this area, communities affected by TB, policy makers and health workers to fully understand the research needs and refine the steps needed to achieve the goal. The project will start with co-design of the AI-POCUS with communities affected by TB, health care providers, and regulators in these settings to understand what they would like from such a product. We will conduct clinical research to determine whether POCUS is an effective and practicable tool for TB screening including which scanning protocol provides the best images, yet can be easily taught and does not overburden health workers or patients, and to start collecting clinical, microbiological and imaging data. To develop the AI reading, large numbers of images and data are needed, however there can be challenges with data privacy and ownership if data is transferred to a central source. The GHRG will therefore conduct research around the broader ethics of data privacy and transfer, and develop capacity to pilot a  federated machine learning approach , which involves all sites retaining full ownership of their data and concurrently training a general machine learning model on-site, before combining these models into a centralised one. The finalised AI-supported POCUS product will then be tested across the four epidemiologically different sites in adults and children being investigated for TB. We will assess the clinical performance and the costs of the system. The GHRG will finally convene a workshop with communities affected by TB and policy makers to present the findings and discuss the roadmap to the further development of the product. We will also produce a training package for health workers to facilitate adoption beyond the facilities and countries in this GHRG . If successful, this product has the potential to be a game-changer for screening of TB in high-burden countries by dramatically increasing access to better quality and co-ordinated TB diagnosis amongst the world's population that are both the most vulnerable to TB and face the greatest barriers to being diagnosed.

title: Systems Engineering and Thinking To Transform Transitions (SET4) in health and care for people with multiple long-term conditions
abstract: More people are living with multiple long-term conditions (MLTC) affecting their health and well-being and these individuals tend to need more health and social care. MLTC become more common in older age, but many younger people are also impacted, particularly in more deprived areas. Previous research talking to people with MLTC has found poorly coordinated services with little communication between professionals involved in a person's care. Patients report systems that manage multiple individual problems rather than providing personalised treatment for individuals. We are particularly interested in the points where responsibility for care changes, known as health and social care transitions. Examples include the transitions between a GP and a specialist hospital clinic or between a hospital and a social care service when discharged home. Our panel of people affected by MLTC told us how difficult it was to coordinate appointments and how the system was not flexible to their more complex needs. Our work aims to identify problems in transitions of health and social care for people with MLTC and to build a new 'Innovation Hub' that will design and launch solutions. Our team comprises clinicians, systems engineers, health and care policy experts and public contributors across South East Scotland and North East England.    Systems Engineering and Systems Thinking are widely used in industry to design change and improvement. These approaches focus on developing a deep understanding of systems, how they interconnect and how people interact with them. We will identify the risks of these systems not working as well as intended and how positive changes to one system may negatively affect others. We are planning three phases over 18 months: 'discovery', 'understanding' and 'design'. In the 'discovery' phase, we will work with patients, carers, health and care professionals and other key groups (like the NHS, social care providers and charities) to identify critical problems for people with MLTC at transitions of care. Activities will involve interviews, focus groups and workshops. We will also find out from these groups what 'good' should look like so that we know what measures to use to test our future solutions. In preparing our application, we already have agreement from many key stakeholders to participate in this work. Tackling health inequalities is critical to our proposal, and we are committed to creating a widely representative panel.   In the second 'understanding' phase, our systems engineers will focus on some key transitions identified in the discovery work. They will map out exactly what happens to people with MLTC and how services interact at these points, using real-world data to understand these transitions. This work will find key targets for research and change in a future Innovation Hub. Our final 'design' phase will focus on the steps needed to create the Hub. We will use co-design, where our patients and other stakeholders will again be involved. We will produce a series of operational and business plans to make sure that a Hub would work well if funded in the future. We have a big vision for an Innovation Hub to be a future leader in health and social care improvement and recognise the need to build capacity to deliver Systems Engineering. We will do this by increasing training programmes for health and care professionals, embedding public involvement throughout, and making expertise available more easily across our regions.

title: Using digital health to transform the management of long-term conditions in the NHS: Assessing real-world patient experience and empowerment and improvements to productivity and capacity
abstract: Background: Healthcare systems face increasing demands for monitoring and treatment of long-term conditions. Remote digital monitoring avoiding hospital visits offers many advantages. During the Covid-19 pandemic safety from transmission has become a major benefit. Itecho has developed the AscelusTM platform, which enables patients to send information through a 'symptom checker' to their clinical team, which reviews this, and the patient s blood tests. Patients then receive encrypted clinical advice, results of blood and other monitoring sent directly to their smart phone/device (Figure 1). Patients deemed at risk are called for face-to-face appointments.  Aims and objectives: To assess, in the real-world setting, how AscelusTM impacts long-term condition management, hospital capacity/productivity and patient experience/empowerment to then support procurement, commercialisation and scale up.   Methods and timelines:  We will assess real-world implementation of AscelusTM in 7 haematological conditions across a comprehensive series of domains in eleven interlinked work packages, encompassing:    Co-design of new digital haematological care pathways, underpinning bespoke platform amendment/integration into hospital IT systems.  Patient validation and safety cohort observational studies, drawn from cohort of 4,560 patients in 3 London and 1 Sheffield site(s).  Evaluation of patient experience and empowerment using focus groups, Ux laboratories, discrete choice experiments and PAM-13 scores.  Economic modelling and cost/benefit analysis.  Mixed methods qualitative study of clinician motivators/barriers to adoption  Feasibility of future AI development for MGUS monitoring.  A new (post-stage 1) work package to assess the enablers and barriers around digital inclusion.   Impact and dissemination: The project will allow patients more convenience and control; hospitals/clinicians to have additional capacity for complex cases; the NHS to save resources. It will also facilitate environmental benefits (less driving/car parking).  Our highly skilled, multi-disciplinary team with academic, commercial, PPI and clinical backgrounds and national leadership roles provides a great opportunity to spearhead digital transformation in haematology across the UK.

title: An artificial intelligence (AI) Macular Disease treatment decision tool for patients with wet age-related macular degeneration, diabetic macular oedema, and retinal vein occlusion.
abstract: Background   Macular Disease (MD) is the leadingcause of preventable sight loss in the developed world.        Successfully tracking the condition is critical to avoiding blindness. But doing so currently demands huge financial and human resources, which is leaving hospital eye departments routinely overstretched and leading to a rise in cases of sight loss.  With the growth in diabetes and life expectancy, demand is expected to soar globally at over 7% per annum exacerbating the problem.     Aims and objectives   Macusoft intelligently triages patients using artificial intelligence (AI) clinical decision support, allowing clinician s to interpret rich diagnostic information easily and reduce unwanted variation from human judgment, thereby creating capacity to see and treat more patients and improve outcomes.  The aim of this project is to develop Macusoft to be able to test it in a clinical environment to ensure it works and is safe, and understand the next steps in R&D leading to eventual commercialisation.     Project plan and methods    The project plans to develop and test Macusoft in a simulation study using anonymised retrospective data from chronic MD patients, and comparing the software triage decision to that of a Consultant Ophthalmologist. title: Regulatory bench-testing of a transformational polymeric heart valve: a key step toward a first-in-human trial to benefit patients aged 18-80 with one valve type
abstract: Research Question: Can we achieve design freeze of a new polymeric heart valve? Background: Worldwide 1.3 million patients with heart valve disease require valve replacement surgery annually. With the geriatric population growing rapidly and rheumatic valve disease affecting 35 million younger patients in undeveloped countries, valve replacement surgeries will increase by 4-5 times by 2050. Existing biological valves (trans-catheter plus surgical devices) are used in 90% of cases. They are biocompatible with excellent functional performance but used only in elderly patients as they last only 10-12 years. Mechanical valves are used in younger patients due to excellent durability but require life-long anticoagulation, which triggers 3-4% thrombo-embolic/haemorrhagic events/year and teratogenicity during pregnancy. These obvious limitations involve poor health outcome and many expensive readmissions. Therefore, we have developed a transformational polymeric heart valve, using a proprietary technology, for patients of any age, that combine excellent durability and biocompatibility with no need for long-term anticoagulation.  Bench testing at ISO standards of 19-21mm aortic valves has demonstrated >35 years of durability with function being similar to the best-in-class biological valve. Short-term in-vivo testing in sheep has confirmed feasibility, function and biocompatibility. Six mitral valves made with the same technology have just been implanted at IMMR-Paris preclinical facility with study design based on FDA and tier 1 company guidance to assess structural integrity, calcification, dynamic performance, biocompatibility, and toxicity at 6-month (results due in April 2022). A spin-out, Cambris Cardiac Ltd, created by Universities of Cambridge and Bristol has secured £450k in seed funding to accelerate the route to adoption and oversee non-clinical/clinical testing required by regulators.   Aims/objectives: To achieve design freeze using methods conforming with ISO 5840:2015 and to progress the device toward NHS adoption. Methods: The research plan includes 3 milestones over 9 working packages (WPs) with Go/No-go criteria: WP1.Material safety validation; Milestone 1:  Acceptable material properties; WP2.Design optimisation; WP3.Standardisation of manufacturing and quality control; WP4.Device validation; Milestone 2:  Design freeze; WP5.Clinical grade coating, sterilisation, packaging and storage; WP6.Development of valve holders and sizers; Milestone 3: In vitro regulatory compliance; WP7.Device description, labelling, performance, and shelf-life specifications; WP8. Health Economics; WP9.Public and patient involvement, engagement and participation (PPIEP). Surveys among 20 patients and 20 heart surgeons/cardiologists/healthcare professionals confirmed clinical need and willingness to receive or implant/assess the new valve and  NHS adoption. The Bristol NIHR BRC PPIEP group have provided feedback captured in the application and we have pre-defined clear PPIEP deliverables.  For risk mitigation we have established partnerships with CamBris Cardiac Limited (co-applicant), Biointeractions-UK (heparin-coating), IMMR-Paris-France (preclinical studies, not funded here), Biomerics LCC-US (material safety/manufacturing, not funded here), Tower Mains Ltd-UK (regulation / quality management system), CardioMed Device Consultants-US (FDA/MHRA regulatory approvals) and Arterius-UK (packaging and shelf life). Timelines: Design freeze by end 2023; preclinical regulatory hurdles cleared by mid 2025; start a FIH trial within 1-year after that. Anticipated Impact, and Dissemination: the new valve could replace existing artificial valves on a global scale, with major patient/societal/economical benefit. Dissemination will be in line with NIHR practice.

title: ImageDx CRC & ImageDx Lung: A centralized, AI-based solution for tissue-based delivery of personalized medicine testing for the NHS.
abstract: Background The 43,000 NHS colorectal cancer (CRC) patients diagnosed yearly require microsatellite instability or mismatch repair testing (MSI/MMR), at a cost of between Â£4,085,000 and Â£8,385,000. Approximately 36,000 patients with non-small cell carcinoma (NSCLC) require PD-L1 testing, costing Â£7M. MSI results take an average of 14 days and PD-L1 delivery is difficult, being based on a pathologist's subjective interpretation. There are geographical gaps across the UK in the delivery of these necessary tests. Aims Our proposal is based on two key pillars: 1. Bringing Artificial Intelligence to routine diagnostics, applied to: a) the basic H&E section, in MSI/MMR, replacing the current PCR/IHC approaches b) objective scoring of PD-L1 IHC. 2. Creating a centralized platform: a) for submission of in-silico images and b) delivery of such algorithms across the NHS. Work Plan We propose work packages to: a) develop and validate the AI algorithms (ImageDx Lung/Colon) on retrospective and prospective datasets. b) create a delivery platform (Sonrai/PMC Central Hub, SPCH) under ISO13485. c) achieve clinical validation and regulatory approval. This novel modality applying AI to diagnostics requires clear explanation to patients, and patient input will be decisive to delivery; a detailed PPI plan is put forward to capture this important contribution. Dissemination and Anticipated Outcomes Dissemination will happen in three phases: a) Northern Ireland. b) PathLAKE membership. c) NHS wide. Our approach will create direct annual savings across the NHS to the tune of Â£648,500   Â£3,228,500. Indirect savings associated with anti-PDL1 therapy based on more accurate testing could impact 10% of the patients and on Â£35M of the budget on therapeutics. Following the NHS drive towards testing centralization, the SPCH will receive online scanned images and render results in 24-48 hours. This model of AI, tissue-based molecular diagnostic delivery will enable adoption of future AI- based testing in the NHS.

title: FRACT-AI: Evaluating the Impact of Artificial Intelligence-Enhanced Image Analysis on the Diagnostic Accuracy of Frontline Clinicians in the Detection of Fractures on Plain X-Ray
abstract: Research question     What is the impact of Artificial Intelligence-enhanced imaging on the diagnostic performance of clinicians who are routinely involved in identifying acute fractures on plain X-Rays?         Background     The missed diagnosis of fractures on X-Ray is the most frequent source of error by clinicians in UK Emergency Departments, and a significant cause of patient morbidity. Initial X-Ray interpretation is typically carried out by Emergency Department clinicians of varying seniority and prior training. Gleamer have developed an Artificial Intelligence-enhanced algorithm (Boneview) which can support clinicians in the detection of fractures on plain X-Ray. Previous research has shown the algorithm to have promising diagnostic performance, but its impact on the diagnostic accuracy of clinicians has not yet been evaluated in the UK healthcare setting.         Aims and Objectives     To evaluate the impact of using Artificial Intelligence-enhanced image analysis on the interpretation performance of clinicians routinely involved in the diagnosis of acute fractures on plain X-Ray.          Methods     We will create a dataset of 500 plain X-Rays involving standard images of all bones other than the skull and cervical spine, with 50% normal cases and 50% containing fractures. A reference  ground truth  for each image to confirm the presence or absence of a fracture will be established by a senior radiologist panel. This dataset will then be inferenced by the Gleamer Boneview algorithm to identify fractures. Performance of the algorithm will be compared against the reference standard.   We will then undertake a Multiple-Reader Multiple-Case study in which clinicians interpret all images without AI and then subsequently with access to the output of the AI algorithm. 18 clinicians will be recruited as readers with 3 from each of six distinct clinical groups: Emergency Medicine, Trauma and Orthopaedic Surgery, Emergency Nurse Practitioners, Physiotherapy, Radiology and Radiographers, with three levels of seniority in each group. Changes in reporting accuracy (sensitivity, specificity), confidence and speed of readers in two sessions will be compared. The results will be analysed in a pooled analysis for all readers as well as for the following subgroups:     Clinical role   Level of seniority  Pathological finding  Difficulty of image          Timelines for delivery     This project will be delivered from July 2023 to February 2024 inclusive         Anticipated Impact and Dissemination     We will generate a detailed assessment of the potential impact of introducing an AI-enhanced fracture detection algorithm on the diagnostic performance of clinicians of varying seniority. This will be used to inform the design of a subsequent large prospective study to fully evaluate their use in clinical practice. Results will be presented to clinical, academic and policy stakeholders at scientific conferences and through publications in scientific journals. We will use patient groups, the National Consortium of Intelligent Medical Imaging, and departmental and University of Oxford channels and online resources to disseminate findings more widely. We will also share the results with relevant stakeholders involved in implementation of AI applications within the NHS

title: Development and randomised feasibility trial of a theory-based digital behaviour change intervention to support self-management for people with Adrenal Insufficiency: the  Support-AI  study
abstract: Research question Is a digital behaviour change intervention feasible and acceptable in supporting self-management in patients with Adrenal Insufficiency?  Background  Adrenal insufficiency (AI) results from cortisol deficiency, a hormone essential for life, caused by failure of the adrenal glands or conditions affecting the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis. Patients with AI require lifelong glucocorticoid replacement. They need to increase glucocorticoids during illness or major stress and require parenteral hydrocortisone in the event of an Adrenal Crisis (AC), mainly precipitated by infections, to prevent hospitalisation and death; these are called 'sick day rules' [4, 5, 7, 8].  Approximately, 1 in 100 patients die and 1 in 12 are hospitalised at least once/year from AC [9, 10]. Almost 4,000 AC-related hospital admissions, at an estimated annual cost of Â£6 million, are recorded every year in the NHS for the 25,000 patients with AI in the UK [11]; half of these could be prevented with improved self-management. Patients with AI have impaired quality of life and high morbidity and mortality [12-14].  A systematic review by the applicant (PROSPERO-CRD42018087632) identified self-management barriers relating to nonadherence to glucocorticoids and 'sick day rules' and other behaviours that aid prevention and treatment of AC, such as AC-symptom awareness, having extra tablets, carrying a medical-alert ID and injection kit, and ability to self-inject. Evidence suggests that existing education programmes are ineffective at improving adherence [15] or reducing AC-related hospitalisations [9, 16]. Therefore, a theory-based self-management intervention focused on behaviour change is needed for patients with AI.  Aim To develop a digital self-management behaviour change intervention for patients with AI, and to evaluate its feasibility and acceptability in a randomised feasibility trial.  Methods  The study, underpinned by the MRC Framework [17], the Behaviour Change Wheel (BCW) [18] and the Person-Based Approach [19], will be conducted in two phases over three years. Phase 1 aims to develop a digital intervention to support self-management for patients with AI. 1a) Informed by the systematic review and ongoing research conducted by the applicant, four focus groups of patients with AI will elicit potential strategies to overcome barriers and enhance enablers to self-management. 1b) BCW methods will be followed to identify potential salient behaviour change techniques and modes of digital delivery. These will be discussed with an Advisory Intervention Panel (10-15 patients, family members, clinicians), using Nominal Group Technique to gain consensus on which should form part of the intervention. A Person-Based Approach using iterative 'think-aloud' technique will guide the development of the website. Phase 2 will test the feasibility, acceptability, and progression criteria of the intervention. A randomised feasibility trial will recruit 80 patients with AI from a university hospital and two patient advocacy groups. Outcome measures will inform a large-scale definitive RCT.  Impact and dissemination Findings will be disseminated to patients and health professionals via scientific/patient conferences, social media, and peer-reviewed publications. The 5-year projected benefit includes cost-effective NHS care (reduced hospitalisations and demand for specialist services) and improved outcomes for patients with AI (QoL, adherence to treatment, reduced hospitalisation, and death from AC).

title: Improving the United Kingdom's pathway for scaphoid fracture diagnosis through automated detection of fractures (the scAIphoid study) and understanding the factors influencing adoption of diagnostic AI.
abstract: Background The scaphoid bone is vital for wrist joint movement and stability. Scaphoid fractures account for 10% of hand, and 60-80% of carpal fractures. Delayed or missed diagnosis greatly increases the risk of post-injury complications, including osteonecrosis, non-union and wrist collapse.    Accurate diagnosis of scaphoid fractures is difficult, as clinical signs and radiographs are unreliable. As a result, patients can be under-treated, leaving them at risk of life-changing complications, or over-treated with unnecessary immobilisation whilst awaiting clinical follow-up and exclusion of possible fracture. Access to more accurate imaging, such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), as recommended by NICE, is limited due to capacity and subject to significant regional variation.    An artificial intelligence (AI) diagnostic aid could improve patient pathways, reduce geographical inequality, and improve the accuracy of scaphoid fracture diagnosis.    Aims     Develop and test the use of an AI model to assist in the detection of scaphoid fractures  Describe barriers to implementation of diagnostic AI in healthcare   Objectives     Develop and validate an AI model to detect scaphoid fractures on radiographs  Evaluate the impact of AI assistance on healthcare professional (HCP) diagnostic accuracy in suspected scaphoid fractures  Investigate the factors influencing adoption of diagnostic AI in clinical practice   Methods   This DRF has three workstreams:  WS1: I will develop and internally validate an AI model to detect scaphoid fractures on radiographs, using 30,000 radiographs obtained from Oxford University Hospitals NHS Trust. I will externally validate the model using images sourced from other NHS Trusts.  WS2: I will perform a Multi-Reader, Multi-Case (MRMC) study to investigate the impact of integrating the model within the diagnostic pathway. I will embed a qualitative study exploring the perspectives of healthcare professionals (HCPs) on using the AI.  WS3: I will describe the barriers and facilitators to adoption of diagnostic AI, through a best-fit framework qualitative evidence synthesis (QES) co-produced with PPI contributors.    Patient and public involvement   PPI contributors have been involved in the development of this proposal, including the design of WS1 and WS2, and the conception of WS3. I will follow GRIPP2 guidelines for reporting my work with PPI contributors and we will share our experience in blog articles and peer-reviewed publications.    Impact   The results of this project will address key research questions identified by UK patients, clinicians and national bodies including the Department of Health and Social Care. Developing, validating and performing a reader study of an AI detecting scaphoid fractures could provide a reliable method to reduce the rate of misdiagnosis in the NHS. Qualitative work, aimed at understanding the barriers and facilitators to adoption of diagnostic AI, could inform future research integrating the AI into patient pathways.    Dissemination   I will publish the key outputs of this work in high-impact, peer-reviewed, international journals. I will present this work at international and national meetings of clinicians (surgeons and radiologists) and academics in the field of hand surgery, medical innovation and artificial intelligence, co-presenting with PPI contributors. I will share my results with the public through project-specific and wider PPI groups, through presentations, infographics and newsletters.
