title: Predicting remission of type 2 diabetes following bariatric surgery: external validation of existing models and model update within the UK primary care electronic health records
abstract: Backgrounds:  Obesity is associated with multiple co-morbidities leading to reduced quality of life and increased health care costs. Bariatric surgery is currently the most effective long-term treatment option for obesity and is associated with lower mortality rates and improved quality of life. But current data suggests that it is not widely accessed or available. Significant disparities exist between patients who are eligible vs patients undergoing bariatric surgery across geographical areas, ethnic groups, and genders. Developing a model with good performance to identify patients with a high likelihood of type 2 diabetes remission and embedding it within the primary care electronic health record could help to improve access for patients seeking treatment for obesity and bariatric surgery.  Aim of our project:  To identify a prediction model to predict diabetes remission with good performance in the UK population with mixed ethnicity and socio-economic status and ensure equity within different patient groups  Methods and data sources:  We will externally validate existing models (DiaRem, DiaRem 2, AdDiaRem, and DiaBetter) to predict type 2 diabetes remission in the UK population. We will use Clinical Practice Research Datalink (CPRD) Aurum and include patients with obesity and type 2 diabetes who had bariatric surgery during the study period from January 2010 to December 2021. We will undertake subgroup analysis based on ethnicity and socioeconomic status defined by the Index of multiple deprivation score (IMD).  Depending on the performance of these prediction models, we will explore the value of using additional variables available within primary care to improve performance in different subgroups and reduce inequalities.  We will use two separate datasets, Clinical Practice Research Datalink (CPRD) Gold and Secure Anonymised Information Linkage (SAIL) Databank, for external validation of the updated prediction model.  Statistical analysis  We will use Stata and R software to conduct the validation study. We will externally validate four available prediction models for predicting diabetes remission at 1, 3, and 5 years. Subgroup analysis will be conducted based on ethnicity and IMD score.  The performance of prediction models will be based on discrimination score, defined as the ability to distinguish between those who will and who will not achieve the outcome of interest, and calibration, defined as the ratio of those expected to have the desired outcome to those observed to achieve the outcome.  We will assess the performance of the prediction models based on measures of discrimination (time-dependent C-statistic), calibration (calibration-in-the-large, calibration slope, and calibration curves), and clinical utility (decision curves).  We will evaluate discrimination and calibration scores for each prediction model for the total population, different ethnicity, and IMD quantile.  Based on our outcome in the external validation study, we will update the best-performing prediction model with new predictor variables to improve the performance in different subgroups. We will undertake an external validation study for the updated prediction model using CPRD Gold and SAIL databank, two separate databases to minimise the risk of overfitting.

title: Using artificial intelligence (AI) to characterize the dynamic inter-relationships between MUltiple Long-term condiTIons and PoLYpharmacy and  across diverse UK populations and inform health care pathways (AI-MULTIPLY)
abstract: Our overarching question is: “How do multiple long-term conditions (multimorbidity)(MLTC-M) and polypharmacy interact and how is this interaction modified by inequalities?”   Background    MLTC-M is associated with premature mortality, significant treatment burden, increased healthcare and socio-economic costs. Deprivation contributes to its early onset while inequalities exacerbate it.  Polypharmacy is associated with MLTC-M but the inter-relationship is complex and poorly understood.  Whereas appropriate polypharmacy may alleviate/prevent disease burden, in other poorly defined circumstances polypharmacy may cause harm.   Aims and objectives Overarching aim: to characterise MLTC-M and polypharmacy (MLTC-M-PP) trajectories and define the inter-relationships between MLTC-M clusters, polypharmacy, inequalities and healthcare outcomes over the life-course.    Specific aims:    Identify early intervention points, including antecedent events prior to  tipping points  associated with rapidly progressive “bursts” of multimorbidity/polypharmacy.  Determine influence of personal and social intersectional factors with the aim of reducing health inequalities.   Define “appropriate” and “inappropriate” polypharmacy in a MLTC-M context.   Initiate emulation of target trials in our target populations.  Demonstrate proof of concept clinical decision support tools based on AI and related technologies to flag MLTC-M-PP risk to health practitioners.  Map the emergence of ideas, assumptions, consensus and knowledge creation in the development of a health-related explainable-AI algorithm, with full consideration of Inequalities.  Foster a reflexive, interdisciplinary learning and training environment.    Data, Methods and Team Our interdisciplinary consortium brings together experts in data access/engineering, epidemiology, pharmacy, clinical medicine, AI, anthropology, trial emulation, PPI, and healthcare relevant to the management of MLTC-M.  Our PPI and stakeholder groups have shaped and extended our research questions and methodologies. Our cutting-edge methodologies include: a novel transfer of Bursty Dynamics theory from complex systems research to characterise healthcare event structure; Association Rules Mining to illuminate event sequence; topological data analysis as a novel approach to understanding complex MLTC-M-PP networks; market-basket analysis with topic modelling to define latent associated conditions; ethnographic analysis of interdisciplinary AI-in-health working practices. Quantitative methods will be optimised using well-curated data (UK-Biobank and CPRD), and then validated on routinely collected electronic health record (EHR) NHS data from the North-East of England and East London, with particular focus on intersectional contrasts, including ethnicity and deprivation. Findings will be interpreted in the local context, with PPI support, and validated in carefully selected cohorts in Bradford and Scotland.   Timelines for delivery 0-18 months: data access and engineering; 0-24 months application of AI methods to deliver MLTC-M-PP clusters; 24-30 months development of clinical decision support systems; 0-30 months: ethnographic analysis and PPI.   Impacts    Increased understanding of MLTC-M-PP clusters in the context of inequality factors and wider intersectional drivers.  Identification of potential 'tipping  points and potential new interventions:     For testing in pragmatic trials.   To support the development of appropriately designed clinical decision support systems.      Enhanced training of early career researchers and capacity building.   Development of guidance for future interdisciplinary AI-in-health collaborations.    Dissemination Informed by consultation with our PPI groups, important findings will be shared widely.  We will facilitate patient, research-partner led discussions across NIHR networks around AI in healthcare including the development of  jargon-bus

title: Understanding mid-life risk and inequalities associated with frailty development in later life: NHS linked records data and prospective cohort analysis from England
abstract: Background Frailty is the most problematic expression of population ageing. It is a state of vulnerability to external stressors that in older people reduces their resilience and ability to deal with stress, illness, or injury. Frail individuals are at greater risk of adverse events, such as falls, hospitalisations, institutionalisation, and death. The prevalence of frailty is expected to rise with an ageing population. Understanding its determinants is crucial for promoting healthy ageing.  Existing prediction models for frailty development are limited and have methodological weaknesses. To date, no reliable prediction model exists to accurately identify patients at high risk of becoming frail in later life.  Aims   To identify mid-life factors associated with frailty development in later life.  To develop and validate clinical prediction models for long-term risk of frailty development in mid-life.  To investigate life expectancy and inequalities in life expectancy in all states of frailty.   I will meet these aims through four objectives:   Systematic review and critical appraisal of existing mid-life individual- and area-level factors associated with frailty development in later life.  Scoping review to identify and investigate methods to evaluate and reduce algorithm bias (fairness) in a clinical prediction model.  Develop and externally validate a clinical prediction model for predicting 20-year risk of frailty among older adults.  Estimate the life expectancy of people in each frailty state according to sex, ethnicity, and area-level socio-economic status in mid-life.   Methods  I will conduct a systematic review to identify mid-life factors associated with frailty development in later life. I will also critically appraise existing prediction models for risk of frailty.  I will develop and validate prediction models using two large UK databases containing primary care electronic patient health records for more than 16 million current patients. I will evaluate different model-building approaches, including machine-learning methods. I will investigate methods to evaluate and reduce algorithm bias to ensure fairness in the developed prediction models.  I will use a longitudinal study that collects data from a representative sample of the English population aged 50 to enrich the models with additional social and psychosocial factors in mid-life.  Expected impact  I anticipate that the research will have a substantial impact within 3 years. It will improve our understanding of the risk and inequalities of frailty in older adults. I will identify the mid-life factors that contribute to frailty development. My findings will help clinicians to identify individuals at high risk of becoming frail in later life, so that they can create more targeted personalised interventions. Establishing whether risk factors are associated with frailty development could help to drive new policies for healthcare, which could include tailored programmes for weight loss or increasing physical activity, for example.  Dissemination  The results will be published in relevant peer-reviewed, open-access journals and presented at national and international conferences. To maximise public engagement, plain language summaries will be produced and shared with my PPI advisory group, patient charities, university websites, and social media platforms.

title: StratCare Trial 2: Evaluating the clinical and cost-effectiveness of AI-driven stratified care for depression
abstract: At least one in six adults in England suffer with depression and anxiety symptoms. Over a million people with these symptoms are referred for talking therapies in the NHS. Most patients are initially offered brief talking therapies lasting around 6 sessions, after which they can access more intensive therapies lasting up to 20 sessions. A problem with this approach is that at least half of these patients don't benefit from brief interventions and either drop out of treatment or end up waiting a long time to access intensive therapies. To address this problem, our team has developed a tool called  StratCare , designed to help NHS services to offer  the right treatment, to the right patient, at the right time . StratCare is a computer programme that guides NHS therapists to ask new patients a few questions about their symptoms and personal characteristics (like age and ethnicity). The system then makes a recommendation for either a brief or an intensive talking therapy available in the NHS. Then the patient can discuss this recommendation with the therapist to decide if it's a good choice for them, or to consider other options. Previous research has found that using the StratCare tool helped more people to recover from depression compared to usual NHS care. In this new study, we will carry out a clinical trial involving several NHS services across England. Some services will use the StratCare tool, and other services will follow the usual approach to recommend talking therapies. We will then contact patients who have agreed to take part in the study to see if their mood and quality of life has improved after 6, 12 and 18 months. We will also interview therapists and patients to see what they think about treatment recommendations being guided by the StratCare tool. This study will help talking therapy services and policy makers to decide if using StratCare helps more patients to recover from depression and if it is affordable for the NHS.

title: Lungy: Development of a Smartphone-based Breathing Management Platform with Integrated Spirometry and Peak Flow Measurement
abstract: Respiratory disease places a huge burden on patients, NHS services and society. The cost of respiratory illness was estimated at £9.9 billion/year (NHS Long-Term Plan), with hospital admissions due to respiratory disease rising at 3x the rate of other admissions and 10,000 new diagnoses of lung disease in the UK every week. Globally, asthma affects more than 300 million people, including 11.6% of children aged 6-7 years, and COPD is the third leading cause of death worldwide. The prevalence of long-COVID in January 2023 was estimated to be 2.1 million people in the UK (with 65 million sufferers worldwide), with 42% of sufferers reporting shortness of breath and 1.6 million reporting impact to their daily lives (ONS, 2023).    Lungy  (https://www.lungy.app) is an accessible and scalable platform that uses a smartphone camera and microphone to recognise, track and respond to real-time breathing data. These data can be used to provide responsive feedback to the patient (and clinician) to aid self-management & telemonitoring of patient progress; to encourage and guide the patient through a range of breathing exercises; and to create unique and relaxing generative audiovisuals that respond to each breath. With further development, the combination of data obtained from facial-tracking and machine learning on audio samples could provide a plastic and hardware-free, eco-friendly alternative to traditional peak flow & spirometry that is always available and accessible to all patients with a smartphone.   Lungy s breath recognition technology has been patented with validation in a proof-of-concept app for patients with stress and anxiety (and no underlying respiratory problems). This app now has over 10,000 active beta testers.  A prototype of a Class I medical device version, for patients with respiratory disease, has been received very positively in patient workshops, focus groups and by the UK's largest breathing charities - Asthma + Lung UK.

title: Crisis care for children and young people with mental health problems: national mapping, models of delivery, sustainability and experience (CAMH-Crisis2)
abstract: Background  There has been a sharp and worrying increase in mental health problems experienced by children and young people. Before the pandemic, one in eight 5-19 year olds in England was likely to have a mental health problem. In 2020, this figure rose to one in six 5-16 year olds. Among those with a mental health difficulty, almost half of older teenagers and a quarter of 11-16 year olds report having self-harmed or attempted suicide. Extreme emotional distress, with or without self-harm, is often referred to as a 'crisis'. Services for young people in crisis are a priority in the UK with services expanding. However, little is known about what crisis services currently exist, who uses them, or what type of service works best for children and young people and their families.  Aim and objectives  This project aims to explore the types of mental health crisis services currently available to children and young people up to the age of 25 in England and Wales, and to examine how they are organised, perceived and integrated within other local care systems.  The objectives are to: 1. Find out what NHS, local authority, education and charity sector crisis services exist for children and young people across England and Wales, to describe the services and to create a database of them. 2. Identify eight contrasting services from the database and evaluate how these services are organised, perceived and integrated within local care systems. 3. Compare and contrast these services with the available international evidence, drawing out clear implications for the design and delivery of future crisis responses for children and young people and their families.  Methods  We will meet objective 1 by using a survey to create a database of crisis response services across England and Wales including how they are organised, implemented and used. To meet objective 2, from the database we will identify eight contrasting services selected for variety in terms of: geography and wealth of the setting (England/Wales, urban/rural, and relative wealth/poverty); populations served (including ethnic diversity); and the nature of the service (including the charity sector and/or social care involvement). Treating each as a case study, we will conduct interviews with children and young people and family members who have used the service as well as managers and staff. We will look at how the services work and gather data on how they are used and by whom. In our analysis we will focus on understanding how each crisis service is provided, perceived and implemented. title: Selecting reablement models that best support people leaving hospital after an unplanned admission
abstract: What is this project about? When people leave hospital, they often need short term support in the community to help them regain abilities to wash and dress themselves, cook, shop or take part in social activities. This kind of support is called 'reablement'. Reablement workers focus on doing activities with, not for, people. Reablement teams can be staffed by homecare workers, by workers specifically trained in reablement but without a homecare background, by homecare workers and occupational therapists, or by mixes of nursing, therapy and homecare staff. Reablement has been around for over a decade, but we are unsure how well it works. We do not know if it works better for some people than others and why, or if the length of time people have support makes a difference. We also do not know much about the type of training that reablement workers get and whether this makes a difference to the experiences and outcomes of the people they are working with. We want to find out which types of reablement help people the most when they leave hospital. What are we going to do? Initially, we will work with 5 areas in England to talk to workers in reablement services and hospitals to understand the service in more detail.  We will also work with people who have used reablement services to develop questionnaires that look at things like quality of life, daily activities, mental health, and use of health and social services. We will ask different types of people about their experiences of receiving reablement. We will speak to people who have had reablement more than once and people who have had more than 6 weeks of reablement. We will hold meetings with representatives of community organisations involved in the health and care system, and advocacy organisations for underserved groups - older people from ethnic minorities and LGBTQ+ communities, people living with dementia, and people living with sensory impairment - about members' experiences of reablement. Based on their feedback, we will explore the experiences of specific underserved groups. We will pay community and advocacy organisations to interview people who have had experiences of reablement and/or their carers and are from underserved groups. The project will have a group of people who have experienced reablement to assist the researchers throughout the study   for instance, to advise whether the questions for people completing questionnaires and interviews make sense and seem appropriate. Using the information that has been collected, we will decide if we can find enough people to complete a larger survey of many more people. We will check whether the questionnaires that we originally used need to be changed to make them easier to answer. If we are confident that enough reablement users and their carers are willing to participate, we will survey people in 8 areas (the original 5 areas, plus another 3). If we are confident that councils can successfully 'link' the survey answers to social services records, we will request and link the data. What will we do with our results? We will use information from survey and care records to work out which types of reablement are best, how much each type costs, and which is the best value for money. We will tell people about our results by publishing academic articles, giving talks to councils, health and community organisations, and publicising our key messages to people who participated in our research so that they know what we've found.

title: Supporting medical students towards careers in general practice: A realist approach to maximising the potential of role modelling in undergraduate medical education.
abstract: Background: A major problem facing UK general practice is inadequate recruitment, particularly in areas of high socio-economic deprivation, and this is impacting on patient care. In order to meet the needs of the population 50% of medical graduates need to become GPs [1], yet actual numbers are closer to 30% [19], inadequate to replace the existing high level of workforce attrition. Role modelling in undergraduate medical education exerts powerful influence on the career choice of future doctors [11,12], but many of those who act as role models are burnt-out and wish to leave the profession [20] [21]. There is an urgent need to consider how those who have greatest impact on the career choices of future doctors can be supported to become positive role model, despite the challenges they face. This research will build on a systematic review and qualitative research undertaken during my NIHR In Practice Fellowship (IPF), and aims to explore how conscious and positive role modelling in undergraduate medical education can be facilitated at individual and institutional level to support medical students towards careers in general practice. Informed by previous research findings realist methods have been selected as they support exploration of complex interventions in policy relevant areas [22].   Research questions: How, why, for whom and in what contexts can GPs be supported to become positive role model to medical students? What is the impact of existing interventions to support positive role modelling on GPs and medical students? In what ways can interventions at individual and institutional level increase conscious and positive role modelling and reduce negative role modelling behaviours.    Methods: An initial explanatory framework (programme theory) linking contexts, mechanisms and outcomes will be developed using outputs from my NIHR IPF. A stakeholder panel including medical undergraduates, GPs and patients from areas of socio-economic deprivation will support this process and provide input at five meetings over the course of the research. A realist review of published and grey literature will be conducted to develop the programme theory and identify knowledge gaps. This will be followed by a realist evaluation using a mixed method approach where surveys, interviews and observations will be undertaken with senior representatives from undergraduate institutions, educators and learners. Interviews and observations will be conducted in educational settings in areas of high socio-economic deprivation in the North East of England, to ensure representation of groups who face significant health inequalities.   Impact and dissemination: Findings will provide an understanding of the experience of GP role models, of actions being undertaken by educational institutions to support positive role modelling, and opportunities for intervention. Using co-creation methods with the stakeholder panel these will be translated into practical recommendations and interventions including a professional report, academic publications, videos and podcasts. These will be shared online, through conferences and social media to ensure maximum impact. Patients and the general practice workforce will benefit from this research as students will be supported towards careers in general practice, and those working in the specialty will receive support to be positive role models.

title: Impact and inequalities of winter pressures in primary care: providing the evidence base for mitigation strategies
abstract: Why are we doing this study? Respiratory viruses are a major reason that GPs are busy in the winter. The major winter viruses are 'flu, Covid-19 and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). We know these viruses cause a large increase in pressure on GPs but exactly what impact GPs being busier has  on people's health is not known. We know respiratory infections don't affect everyone equally and that people with lower incomes or of ethnic minority backgrounds both catch more viruses and have worse outcomes if they do. People from lower incomes and minority groups also tend to have poorer access to GPs and so may be particularly impacted when GPs get very busy. Vaccines can reduce the impact of infections, and are available for these viruses but we know that access and uptake of these vaccines is also reduced in people from lower income groups and minority ethnic backgrounds. For all of these reasons the pressure that GPs are under in winter might impact some people more than others.  Aims This project aims to understand:   - The impact of wintertime pressures on GP practices   - How GPs being busier affects patient health    - If the impacts are different for patients in different income and ethnicity groups   - If increasing vaccination coverage could reduce these impacts  How were patients involved in developing this study? Patient and public representatives helped develop this proposal; informing the way we will do the study and how we will involve patients during the project. We will make a patient advisory group (PPI AG) to provide feedback throughout the project. With these patient advisors we will develop surveys and focus groups to capture the experiences of GP practice staff and people of diverse backgrounds. Patient advisors will have many opportunities to contribute including helping write scientific papers and developing material to share our findings in language non-scientists can understand. We also spoke to GPs about why they think they get busier in the winter and differences between practices. We will hold more workshops with GPs and other healthcare professionals to help us carry out the study and understand our findings.   What will we do? We will access health records using a secure computer system. Using these records we will learn new information about the pressures the NHS faces in the winter. This includes which symptoms patients see the GP for at different times of year, which patient groups are most affected when GPs get busier and how this varies between GP practices. We will try to find signs that a GP practice is becoming too busy ('overwhelmed'), such as increasing delays in the time to appointments. We will see if patients  are more likely to go to hospital or have severe health events when GPs are busy. We will use mathematical models of the population to see how demographic factors (such as ethnicity) and the fact that some groups have lower vaccine coverage affect whether their GPs become particularly busy. We will include other factors that could affect people differently where they live, like the type or density of housing. We will also test different ways (e.g. prioritising different groups for vaccination) to reduce the infections in the community.    What difference this will make? By better understanding why some GPs and some populations are more affected by pressure in the winter, we hope to find ways to reduce the impact of respiratory infections, tackle health inequalities and improve health outcomes.

title: Assessment of a unique AI-enhanced clinical support platform to streamline Urgent Treatment Center clinical decision making
abstract: Urgent Treatment Centres (UTCs) provide a community alternative to Emergency Departments for serious, non-life-threatening illness. They play a pivotal role in primary care by reducing avoidable hospital admissions as well as supporting many underserved populations who tend not to access registered general practice[1]. Facing rising patient demand, UTCs are upskilling their nurse-led clinical teams, extending their scope of practice and augmenting the team with paramedics[2,3,4]. These practitioners need extensive knowledge across conditions and awareness of updated protocols and services for their expanded roles and are often requiring senior input, leading to inefficient workflows, inconsistent patient delivery, and delayed care[5-10].  Homerton Primary Urgent Care Centre (PUCC), rated 'outstanding' by the CareQualityCommision, are seeking to partner with DemDx,  a regulated medical device health technology company, to assess whether a UTC tailored AI-enhanced clinical support platform could augment practitioners clinical confidence, reduce the supervision burden and streamline the PUCC service for patients. This project aligns with the FAST grant scope of seeking to improve primary care demand management, the identification of high-risk patients, and prevention of unnecessary hospital admissions. DemDx s existing Class 1 certified GP-CAP platform is already deployed in two separate Integrated Care Systems in General Practice surgeries and fully complies with NHS digital standards (DTAC). It has demonstrated clinical/operational benefits with a 30% reduction in patient time-to-assessment and an 85% increase in adherence to gold standards protocols. Patient panels have been involved throughout the development of the platform, including providing key insights on how best to deploy the platform within the clinical setting to optimise patient acceptance.   DemDx has leveraged this existing technology to develop an early prototype (TLR3) UTC-tailored AI clinical support platform (AI-UTP) specifically addressing acute minor illness presentations ready for critical clinical and user testing.

title: Clinical validation of the AI Clinician decision support system for sepsis treatment
abstract: Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction due to severe infection and affects 250,000 patients annually in the UK, of whom 48,000 die. In addition, virtually all Covid-19 intensive care unit (ICU) deaths had sepsis. As part of ICU treatment, the cornerstone of sepsis resuscitation is the administration of intravenous fluids and/or vasopressors to maintain blood flow to prevent organ failure. However, uncertainty around correct dosing and timing of treatments, partially due to clinical syndrome heterogeneity, leads to poorer outcomes and increased ICU-resource use. We tackle this problem using an AI that learned from ICU electronic healthcare records to provide personalised treatment recommendations to clinicians. Our AI recommender system, the “AI Clinician”, extracted implicit knowledge from large ICU-databases and learned optimal sepsis treatment by analysing myriads of clinical decisions. We demonstrated in proof-of-principle retrospective studies that our AI s treatment strategy was on average better than clinicians: In a 100,000-patient validation cohort, patient mortality was lowest where clinicians  actual doses matched AI recommendations: mortality rates rose, in a dose-dependent manner, as clinicians  actual decisions diverged from AI recommendations. Thus, the 3 our technology s competitive advantages are that it can 1) extract relevant knowledge from our data sets, which are much larger than human clinicians could experience in a lifetime; 2) learn optimal strategies from suboptimal previous clinical decision examples; 3) optimise sequential decisions in real-time as patient conditions evolve. Our AI technology requires now prospective validation in relevant, operational environments - we propose this in four ICUs across two NHS trusts. Therefore, we will build a software platform capable of interfacing with many different NHS/ICU IT systems and running our AI algorithm in real-time, to provide dosing suggestions and their justifications to ICU physicians. We will protect intellectual property and follow the processes for medical device software regulation to allow certification and commercialisation.

title: Assessing the acceptability of an enhanced AI platform to directly influence clinical outcomes for users/patients experiencing domestic abuse, within existing NHS pathways.
abstract: The GetOutGetLove Programme (GOGL) is a long-term (6 to 12 months) digital recovery programme (currently website delivered) for adults who have left domestic abuse (DA).  DA consequences are estimated to cost the NHS £2.3bn per annum1 and the wider UK economy £66bn per annum2.  Half a million6 patients seek NHS services each year for DA – with pathways into DA services, commissioned pathfinders, charities or onto mental health services.  Waiting times range from 3 to 23 months in the SW, with known mental health risks during these periods3,4. Almost all services offer short term programmes or therapy only.  From our research there are no specific digital interventions, that support DA patients who are in recovery5those that do exist support exit and access to helplines or paid counsellors.   GOGL provides a comprehensive journey for people at three stages in relation to DA (escaping, recently escaped and long-term out).  It is designed by Dr Craig Newman (Clinical Psychologist), soon to be published as an international self-help book (by Hodder & Stoughton) and already developed into a digital programme.  The health problem is addressed by meeting the gaps in the existing pathways:    Private and confidential.  Self-paced and accessible 24/7.  Inclusive to all genders, ages and sexes (many services are gender specific).  Low cost and scalable.  Long-term.  Intelligent monitoring.   The programme has been developed via research and qualitative PPI involvement (charities, service users, clinicians and feedback and model critique with sector providers), over 3 years.  Market proof is currently being explored via an Innovate UK FAST fund with 5 charities and 32 market acceptability participants (ending April 2023) alongside market analysis.    This application is to assess the specific acceptability, to NHS patients in DA pathways, of a recovery programme with developed AI supported assessment and monitoring.

title: What are the most beneficial models used by community food assets to prevent the need for emergency food aid? A longitudinal qualitative study conducted in two multi-cultural populations in the North and South of England
abstract: Background: One in five families with children in the UK live in a household where they cannot regularly access affordable and healthy food, known as 'food insecurity'. This negatively affects physical and mental health. Organisations across the UK called 'community food assets' provide support with emergency food and/or by preventing people needing emergency food. This might be done, for example, by helping people to claim available benefits or providing credit for their utility bills. Only about half of those who need support use a food asset, in part because people feel ashamed. Local and national government have asked us to identify which types of food assets are best at preventing people needing emergency food and what it is specifically that they do to help people who are food insecure. We will also look at how easy food assets are to approach and whether they support everyone in need.  Aim: To investigate what approaches used by community food assets are most likely to help prevent the need for emergency food in two multi-cultural populations in the North and South of England and use the research to inform local and national government as to how best to invest in these or other resources.  Methods: Research in Bradford and Tower Hamlets (London): 1: Researchers will listen to food asset users and people working in voluntary organisations and local governments to understand how different organisations work together and the role they play in peoples' lives. This will produce a picture of the complex food aid system, highlighting the pathways and processes through which food assets help (or hinder) to prevent food insecurity.  2: Over 12 months, researchers will work as volunteers at five food assets to understand how they work and to meet users, volunteers and staff. After three months, researchers will carry out 'go-along' interviews with families, spending time with them to understand their lives and the role food assets play. Researchers will also spend time with families who are food insecure but do not use food assets to understand why, and how they manage. All families will take photos, videos and other media of things that are important to them about food. All the above will help us understand which food assets approaches are most effective (how and in what ways) and how accessible and inclusive they are.  3: Throughout the project, we will consider how our findings are able to make the biggest difference; from ensuring our questions are of need, choosing our methods and sharing our results to change policy.  Public involvement: People receiving food aid and those working in local government, voluntary organisations and food assets have all told us that this research is essential. We changed our original plans to make sure that researchers volunteered within food assets to build trust with people using them. We will continue to work alongside food asset users and our project team includes someone who is food insecure.  Impact/dissemination: Part 3 of our methods (above) has been developed specifically to ensure that our research can make the biggest difference. We will provide regular updates and findings to everyone involved, including local and national government, voluntary organisations, communities and academics. These will be tailored to the audience and will highlight which food asset approaches prevent the need for emergency food. We will also host public exhibitions of the photos/videos that families shared with us.

title: Why are we stuck in hospital? Understanding service user, family and staff perspectives when transforming care for people with learning disabilities and/or autism
abstract: In recent years, there has been growing concern about the number of people with learning disabilities and/or autism living in long-stay hospitals. Although the UK decided to close asylums for people with learning disabilities from the 1960s onwards, there has been a growth in people admitted to so-called 'assessment and treatment units', with allegations that some people stay here for far too long, with little 'assessment' or 'treatment' that could not be provided elsewhere. Other people live in secure units or in an NHS campus where the previous hospital is still in the process of closing. Over 2,100 people live like this at the moment (despite repeated policies to help people leave hospital and live in the community). This is a real problem as these services struggle to help people to lead ordinary lives, are very expensive, can be a long way from people's homes and families, and have seen a number of abuse scandals   just as was the case with the asylums of the 1960s.    Despite this, there has been little research on why people with learning disabilities are delayed in such settings. In particular, previous debates have often failed to talk directly to people with learning disabilities, their families and front-line staff about their experiences of living or working in such settings, what they see as the main barriers and what would help more people to leave hospital. In other research with older people, we have looked at these issues from the perspective of older people themselves, their families and care staff, as each group has a unique view on what is happening and might make a difference. Unless we listen to these voices we will not find solutions to these problems, and too many people will remain in hospital unnecessarily. Our aim here is to do the same with people with learning disabilities, their families and care staff, so that their voices are heard too. This will increase the chance that people can leave hospital in a timely way and lead more ordinary lives in the community.    This is sensitive work, requiring skills in working with people who may not communicate verbally, where there is a risk that some people can be violent (as all of us can when we're scared and distressed), and where there can be tensions around what is best. We have therefore included a skilled, experienced team who can carry out such in-depth work in a way that suits the needs of the individual. We also have strong relationships with local services, national policy and voluntary agencies working with people with learning disabilities in long-stay hospitals   and these will be crucial for the study's success.    We will produce a report and articles so that people can read what we have found. We will also produce a good practice guide (based on the experiences of people with learning disabilities and their families) and send this to every health and social care leader in the country. We will also produce a free training video for care staff who may not have access to as much training/support as they need. We will ensure our research is conducted well and produces helpful findings by working with a group of national advisors, chaired by a person with a learning disability. We will design our research materials with a group of people with learning disabilities and families, so that the questions we ask, how we get to know people and how we share our findings work really well for people with learning disabilities and their families.

title: AI-enabled point-of-care technology for radiotherapy planning peer review
abstract: Background  Approximately 50% of cancer patients are offered radiotherapy treatment. An important part of radiotherapy planning involves delineating (“contouring”) the target to be irradiated; a complex and time-consuming process. As such, the Royal College of Radiologists advocates peer-review of contours to ensure quality. However, peer review is frequently not performed owing to resource constraints.  Aims  The aim of this project is to investigate the technical and clinical feasibility of an automatic artificial-peer-review software, a system to screen contouring for potential errors. The project will aim to find the most appropriate format to deploy the system clinically, and to establish if it is technically feasible to flag likely errors and to provide a clinically useful explanation of why.  Project Plan  The clinical feasibility study will be undertaken by the University of Manchester, which will involve two contouring workshops; to gather feedback from clinicians on the design, and subsequently their experience, of the artificial-peer-review concept. The technical feasibility study will be undertaken by Mirada Medical, who will investigate the viability of encoding contouring guidelines into a deep-learning model to provide  feedback.  Timelines  The project will last 12 months. The first workshop will be held within 3 months, and the second will take place in the final two months.  Impact and Dissemination  The project output, which will be the proof-of-concept automatic artificial-peer-review software, will be disseminated by demonstration to the clinicians during the final workshop. The Technical results will be made available in an open access publication. Results will also be made available to the general public via the website  radiotherapy and me . The project will provide evidence to support investment in and development of the concept into a clinical prototype, to further the potential of the technology for longer term clinical benefits.

title: Which health visiting models in England are most promising for mitigating the harms of maternal related Adverse Child Experiences?
abstract: As many as 1 in 10 children in England currently live with parents who are violent or abusive to each other, who misuse alcohol or drugs, or who have mental health problems. In our study we focus on children who live with these types of experiences, which have been called 'adverse childhood experiences' or 'ACEs' for short. There are lots of different types of ACEs, for example parents splitting up or a family member going into prison. All ACEs are events or  situations which are probably traumatic or extremely  stressful for a child. We are only looking at families where we can tell whether the mother has experienced serious violence, used  drugs or alcohol at a serious level or has had serious mental health problems. Although fathers are a very important part of the family picture, we cannot 'find'  fathers in the data we use so our focus is on mothers.     Children who have lived with  ACEs tend to have worse health and wellbeing than other children and this often carries on as they become teenagers and grow into adults. Children who grow up with ACEs whilst also living in poor households tend to have particularly worse health and wellbeing. The first years of life are key for health and development and helping children with ACEs before school can stop problems getting worse for these children and improve their health and wellbeing in the short and long term.       Health visitors are qualified public health nurses whose job it is to support all families with their young children's health, including families where there are ACEs. Health visitors work in a 'health visiting team' with others, including nurses with less specialist qualifications or nursery nurses who have child care and education diplomas.  The health visiting team gives advice, support and guidance to parents of young children about a broad range of child health issues. They work with other professionals such as social workers and doctors and often put families in touch with other services which can help them, such as parenting groups, charities or professionals who can help with a child's speech and communication. The government says that every family in England should see a health visitor five times before a child is three years old and that those living with ACEs should get a lot more support from the health visiting team (and also social workers and other professionals). Seeing a family often is the way that the health visiting team can  build a trusting relationship with parents, support parents to tackle their problems, help change things in the family that are not helpful for the child and encourage a strong bond between the parents and the baby or young child.     We do not know the best ways of balancing health visiting for all families with health visiting that targets support to families most likely to be living with ACEs (e.g. those in the poorest neighbourhoods in England). Health visiting is organised differently across England and many families, including those with ACEs, do not see their health visitor as often as the government says they should. Our research will help us understand which ways of organising health visiting are most promising for helping families with ACEs, and whether they are only likely to work in specific contexts, such in areas with a children's centre or where there are enough health visitors for the number of families in an area. This research could be used by the government as it is making changes to health visiting and by local leaders in each council in England who are designing services for babies and very young children in their area.     We will use national information from health visiting services and hospitals as well as information on what types of families live in  local areas to describe how often health visitors see families and whether they visit some families more than others.  As the national information only contains basic (and sometimes incomplete) details of health visiting and families,  we will also carry out a survey and interviews with professionals and mothers to understand the full picture, including what services are used, how often, how the services might help families with ACEs, and how much the services cost the government. We will also talk to three different groups of mothers, for example women who have experienced domestic violence. WE will also speak to one group of young men who are fathers and have experience of some of the ACEs we are looking at.  We will put all this information together to describe what is currently being done in England, for whom, at what cost, and why. We anticipate that we will find between 3 and 5 different 'ways' (models) of providing health visiting in England.     We will then use the national information to see if particular ways (models) of heath visiting appear better than others for helping children with ACEs, for example by improving  child development, or reducing the number of times children or their mothers have a hospital stay  because of alcohol or drugs , domestic violence, or mental health problems (mother)  or accidents or illnesses (child). In the final year of the study (year 4) we will interpret check our results still make sense, given that COVID-19 has changed the way that families live and that health professionals work.  We will check if the government is collecting the most useful information to monitor health visiting and will produce evidence briefings to support people making decisions about how to organise health visiting at national and local levels.

title: MendelScan - An innovative AI case-finding platform to accelerate the diagnosis of rare diseases using primary care electronic health records
abstract: Background MendelScan has shown significant promise in: (1) detecting RD patients earlier than the current standard of care in retrospective studies on research datasets; and (2) detecting previously undiagnosed patients with very high probability of RD diagnosis on real world cohorts of c.200,000 NHS patients. Aims and Objectives This study aims to build on these initial findings to evaluate in real world NHS settings whether (vs current standard of care) MendelScan can: Reduce time-to-diagnosis for RD patients Increase overall RD diagnosis rates (find previously undiagnosed patients) Reduce avoidable healthcare activity associated with the pre-diagnosis phase for RD patients Be implemented practically, ethically and affordably within the NHS Work plan Four phases: Retrospective algorithm validation. Evaluating sensitivity, specificity and positive predictive value of RD case-finding algorithms by running them on very large research datasets (13m patients) of already-diagnosed RD patients. Implementation research. Studies on ethical and practical deployment issues including user acceptability, exploring the right user target and resource-intensity of deployment. Real world data collection. Deployment of MendelScan in real world primary care settings (initially 10 PCNs/practice groups, 750k patients, with potential to extend to c. 2m) to collect data on acceptance of recommendations by GPs, referrals, diagnoses, and resources / activity in the pre-diagnosis phase. Prospective research study, under protocol. Formal evaluation of the MendelScan tool using the NHS Clinical Research Network assessing the tool's impact on diagnosis rates, time to diagnosis, and resource-intensity of the pre-diagnosis phase (vs current standard of care). Timelines for delivery 18 months. Phases 1-3, first 9 months, Phase 4 month 10-16. Evaluation and dissemination months 16-18. Anticipated Impact and Dissemination The study is designed to create the efficacy, economics and acceptability evidence base to justify broad national commissioning. Exit strategy after funding Deployment of MendelScan through ICSs (via PCNs) across the NHS.

title: Early Laser for Burn Scars (ELABS) - A prospective randomised, controlled trial (RCT) to study the effectiveness of the treatment of hypertrophic burn scars with Pulsed Dye Laser (PDL) and standard care compared to standard care alone
abstract: Research question  Does the treatment of hypertrophic burn scars with pulsed dye laser during the early stages of scar formation improve both scar quality/appearance and quality of life (QoL) as assessed by the patient?  Background  Hypertrophic scars are abnormal scars that are red, raised and firm.  These scars can occur following burn injury and, as survival rates from burns have improved significantly, an increasing number of burn survivors go on to live with expansive, life-changing hypertrophic scars.  This residual scarring often needs further treatment to improve the outcome; functionally, aesthetically and psychologically.  Aims and objectives The aim is to assess the effectiveness of treating hypertrophic burns scars with pulsed dye laser (PDL) at an early stage of scar formation.  The objective is to improve QoL for the patient by improving both the appearance and quality of burn scarring, as well as reducing its psychological and psycho-social impact.  The study will also evaluate both the cost-effectiveness and the patient-reported experience of the treatment.   Methods  This is a parallel-arm randomised, controlled trial to compare PDL and standard care against standard care alone.  The difference is measured between baseline and 6 month follow-up.  The recruits are within 3 months of healing from a burn injury; with wounds showing a defined potential for hypertrophic scarring.  A total of 150 patients will be recruited in a multi-centre study at 7 burns units/centres across the UK.  They are randomised in a 1:1 allocation to each arm.  This detects the required effect size with 90% power.  The treatment arm receive 3 PDL treatments at 6 week intervals in addition to standard care, whereas the control arm receives standard care alone.    The primary outcome is the patient-rated part of the Patient and Observer Scar Scale (POSAS).  Psychological and psycho-social impact is evaluated using the CARe burn scale (UWE, Bristol) and Quality Adjusted Life Years (QALY) is determined using the Short-Form Health Survey (SF-12).  Blinded assessments include an objective measurement of the difference in scar redness at follow-up and observer-rated scar quality.  Scar colour is measured objectively using a colorimeter.  An economic analysis assesses the cost-effectiveness of this treatment.  Qualitative interviews after follow-up identifies themes in the patient experience of the treatment process and its effectiveness in ameliorating the impact of scars.  The adverse effect profile of the treatment is also mapped.  Timelines for delivery  This is a study of 36 months duration:    3 months trial set-up  21 months recruitment  6 months follow-up  6 months of data analysis and publication of reports   Anticipated impact and dissemination Results from this study are disseminated to Healthcare Professionals through publications in journals and presentations at relevant burns and scar conferences nationally and internationally.  The qualitative component is published within an open access journal such as BMJ (Open).  It is anticipated that the research output will contribute towards a novel NICE guideline on the laser treatment of burn scars.  It will produce a robust PDL treatment protocol that can be shared across the UK Burns Network, and possibly globally.

title: Guidance for health economic modellers for incorporating individual and aggregate behaviour into models of Public Health interventions
abstract: Background Commissioners of Public Health interventions need to decide where best to spend their money in order to maximise health gains and/or reduce health inequalities. Health economic models use evidence from multiple sources to predict all important differences in outcomes between the intervention(s) and current practice, which can inform policy decisions. Health economic models of behaviour-change interventions typically either exclude behaviour from the model, including only risk factors such as cholesterol, or they make simplified assumptions based on limited or no evidence, for example that behaviour remains constant over each individual's lifetime. However, in other disciplines, like psychology, theories have been developed to try to explain how and why an individual's behaviour changes. In other disciplines, like sociology, different types of models are used to predict the behaviour of a group based on understanding the behaviour of individuals and their interaction with their environment. Model predictions could be improved by drawing upon research from these other disciplines, which would decrease the risk of making wrong decisions about how best to spend limited public funds.  Aims and objectives  The aim of the research is to develop guidance for health economic modellers for incorporating behaviour into models which compare the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of behaviour-change interventions. The guidance will consider modelling of individual behaviours and the impact of social groupings and factors within a person's environment upon their behaviour. This will provide modellers with tools to make better predictions.  Specific objectives are:   To identify and critically review existing methods for incorporating behaviour within quantitative models (across disciplines).  To use an iterative approach to develop a taxonomy of methods for modelling individual and aggregate behaviour within health economic models of behaviour-change interventions, setting out requirements for each method including data, resources and technical skill.  To test the taxonomy and methods within case studies assessing the cost-effectiveness of behaviour-change interventions in order to improve them.  To extend an existing conceptual modelling framework of Public Health interventions to provide guidance to health economic modellers about incorporating behaviour into a health economic model.  To disseminate the research to modellers, decision makers and members of the public.   Anticipated impact and dissemination  This research has the potential to improve predictions of the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of behaviour-change interventions, and hence improve resource allocation decisions. This would result in improved health and wellbeing of the general public overall. It could also facilitate decisions about targeting specific populations, hence aiming to reduce inequalities.  The research findings will be disseminated via a broad range of methods, including presenting at conferences, publishing in high impact peer-reviewed journals, within ScHARR and collaborators' websites, commissioners' forums, and other social media (eg. via existing blogs and twitter accounts). I will connect with relevant commissioning bodies and academic departments throughout the project with the aim of increasing the impact of the research. I will consult with stakeholders, including public representatives, to understand the best approach to dissemination to achieve the biggest impact of the research.

title: Translating a novel AI-based tool for segmenting ovarian cancer on CT scans into clinical care: is it clinically useful and will patients trust it?
abstract: Ovarian cancer is the most common cause of gynaecological cancer death worldwide(1). Lack of progress in survival-outcome over the last 30 years is partly due to difficulty establishing whether patients are responding to treatment. On CT-scans, the primary imaging-modality in ovarian cancer, this assessment is made by measuring the change in length of a few randomly selected tumours. This, however, does not work well for complex diseases like ovarian cancer because response to chemotherapy can vary greatly across multiple disease-sites, which are present in 60% of newly-diagnosed patients(1,2,3).   Our team has developed an automated segmentation tool which identifies and delineates all tumour sites on CT-scans, which is usually too time-consuming for a radiologist to perform manually. It measures the volume of every tumour-site, the combined volume across all tumour-sites, and automatically calculates any change in response to treatment. In complex cancers like ovarian cancer this approach is more accurate at measuring response to treatment than measuring change in tumour length(3,4).   Our next step is to perform a clinical feasibility study. We developed a framework for the qualitative evaluation of segmentation tools, called AUGMENT (Assessing Utility of seGMEntation Tools) which uses the insights of an expert clinician. AUGMENT assesses the AI s segmentation performance alone and when assisting a radiologist, and we have found in recent, unpublished research that using AUGMENT gives a better understanding of clinical-utility than using the standard statistical metrics like Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) alone.  We have performed extensive PPI work on our tool to gauge how patients feel about using it in their care. We conducted over 30 hours of 1-to-1 interviews with patients who had been diagnosed with ovarian cancer. Before they would accept the tool, patients wanted their clinicians to understand its functioning and to trust its performance.

title: Evaluating the implementation of the Transforming Children and Young People's Mental Health Provision Green Paper
abstract: In 2017, the Department of Health and Department for Education published plans to improve support for children and young people experiencing poor mental health. There are three key parts to the programme:    1. encouraging schools and further education colleges to select a member of staff to lead on mental health and wellbeing;    2. creating new mental health support teams (MHSTs) to help schools and colleges promote mental wellbeing for all, and directly help children with mild to moderate mental health problems; and    3. testing how to achieve a maximum waiting time of four weeks for children and young people to access specialist help. The plans also involve creating and training a new workforce of 'education mental health practitioners' who will work in MHSTs.       An early evaluation was carried out to understand how well the programme was working. This reported good progress and found that schools and colleges welcomed having additional mental health support. There were also challenges, including that: some children had mental health problems that were too serious for the new teams to manage easily, but not serious enough to be accepted for specialist support; and some education mental health practitioners moved on from the teams quite quickly after they had been trained, leaving teams short-staffed.       The National Institute for Health Research is funding a longer-term evaluation to understand what difference the programme is making to: children, young people, and their parents or carers; schools and colleges; mental health services; and the way in which different professionals and services work together to support children's wellbeing and mental health. We are a team of researchers from London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, University of Birmingham, University of Cambridge and RAND Europe. We plan to gather and make sense of data that have already been collected (from the NHS, schools and colleges), as well as collecting additional data using surveys, self-completion questionnaires, group interviews and one-to-one interviews.       We will find out about children and young people's experiences of receiving help from an MHST, and about the teams' experiences of providing help. We will also talk to staff in schools and colleges to find out if the programme has helped them to support the wellbeing of children and young people in their setting, including those who have not received individual help from an MHST. We will explore any such  whole-school effects  to understand how things have changed within schools and colleges. We will also explore the different ways that local areas involved in the programme are providing their MHST service, and what they have learned from this. We will try to understand the costs of setting up and delivering the service.        The research team will work closely with children, young people, parents and carers to design and deliver the study, including training young people as co-researchers to undertake group interviews in schools and colleges. The team will be supported by the National Children's Bureau, who will provide advice on how to carry out the research and how to communicate the findings in appealing, accessible and effective ways. We will share findings in a number of ways including reports, conference presentations, an animated video, academic articles, through social media, and will also tell those involved in the programme at all levels what we have found.

title: BRAIN AI: Biomarker Research to Assess Inflammation in Neurodegeneration using Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Background  Early diagnosis of dementia allows for prompt medical management which helps preserve the patient's cognition, daily function and quality of life for longer. Dementia diagnosis often requires multiple investigations, including cognitive assessments, blood and/or cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) tests and neuroimaging.  Despite this wide-range of techniques currently at our disposal, diagnosis remains a highly subjective and lengthy process. There is strong demand from the clinical community for objective tools to enable early dementia diagnosis. Neuroimaging studies show that reduced brain perfusion is an early functional marker of dementia. In addition, new evidence implicates inflammation as a driving force for neurodegeneration. Blood and CSF biomarkers of inflammation, some of which were pioneered by researchers in Southampton, are associated with accelerated progression of dementia. The quantitative combination of these diagnostic techniques could support earlier diagnosis of dementia.  Aim  To evaluate the role of routine clinical and targeted biomarkers of inflammation in dementia progression and identify neuroimaging signatures of the impact of inflammation on brain perfusion.   To exploit the added value of using inflammation markers for dementia prognosis by combining them with neuroimaging and patient demographics using a quantitative diagnosis support tool that will facilitate objective diagnosis of dementia.     Methods  This study proposes secondary analysis of data from a cohort of 446 patients at University Hospital Southampton collected during the NIHR-funded Brain Imaging in Dementia (BRAIID) study, which focused on optimising the use of imaging data for diagnosis and prognosis. BRAIID includes data on neuroimaging, patient demographics and blood/CSF results, presenting a unique opportunity for multiparametric analysis.  Targeted biomarkers including cytokines and vascular markers will be measured in BRAIID CSF samples using assay kits. Secondary data analysis of routine biomarkers from previously assayed blood and CSF samples will also be performed. Functional brain perfusion imaging data will be analysed using statistical parametric mapping to identify neuroimaging signatures of inflammation in patients with high vs low burden of inflammation. To harvest the complementary nature of inflammation markers, neuroimaging and patient demographics, these data will be quantitatively combined into a diagnosis support tool using Artificial Intelligence techniques. The tool will be trained and validated on clinical data from BRAIID, to support future integration into dementia care pathways, with input from patients and clinicians to direct its development most appropriately.    Impact, timelines for delivery and dissemination   This research will provide:   Neuroimaging signatures of routine (publication by Mar. 2022) and targeted (publication by Nov. 2023) biomarkers of inflammation. These signatures will provide new insights into the impact of inflammation on brain function, highlighting the areas of the brain most affected and expanding our understanding of dementia pathophysiology and progression in the presence of inflammation  A quantitative diagnosis support tool for objective assessment of dementia (Complete evaluation using BRAIID cohort data and publish outcomes by Aug 2024).  Dissemination will be achieved through:   Open-access publishing in reputable scientific journals  Presentation of results in scientific conferences  Participation in Patient and Public Involvement engagement events  Visiting other NHS Trusts to share knowledge and methods, and to cross-validate the developed techniques.

title: NIHR Global Health Research Group on Transforming Parkinson's Care in Africa (TraPCAf)
abstract: The largest proportionate growth of people aged over 60 is occurring in low & middle income countries (LMICs), such as those in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). Already coping with a large burden of infectious diseases they now face a large increase in age-related diseases such as dementia and Parkinson's disease (PD). There are very few medical specialists.  We estimate half the people with PD (PwP) in the world are not diagnosed. Effective symptomatic drug treatment is available, though not a cure, but access is very limited in SSA. People undiagnosed, and others not treated, will have a much poorer quality of life and a significantly reduced life expectancy. We have treated people in SSA who were virtually bed bound and within days were back working on their farm. We showed similarly dramatic short term impacts for a physiotherapy cueing intervention before drug treatment was available locally.  There is a lack of awareness about PD among the general public and health professionals, so people often don't recognise symptoms or access medical help and, even when they do, may not be correctly diagnosed. Some PwP see traditional, or faith, healers and many seek no help at all, mistaking the symptoms for old age and feeling nothing can help. Even those diagnosed face the challenge of obtaining affordable and sustainable drug treatment.     This research will enable us to gain important information on PD and effectiveness of treatment in Africa. We will test ideas for helping diagnosis and management, and develop support including patient and carer information. We will strengthen research capability in PD in Africa. We are linking with a current research study looking at the genetics of PD worldwide, including Africa.      We plan to work with colleagues in Tanzania, Kenya, Ghana, Nigeria, South Africa, Ethiopia and Egypt to:   Improve Diagnosis    1. Develop aids to diagnosis for non-specialist doctors, such as questionnaires appropriate for LMIC settings, and equipment that measures slowness of movement and tremor, the two major symptoms of PD. We will utilise new techniques such as scripted videos recorded on smartphones and then analysed by movement disorder specialists in Africa, UK or Europe, and also investigate chemicals in blood, sweat and urine as early signs of PD.  2. Provide training for doctors, nurses and therapists to improve diagnosis and management.  3. Develop and trial services for diagnosis and management of PD by non-specialists.  4. Undertake community based studies of the number of people with PD (prevalence) in Tanzania, Ghana, Nigeria and Kenya, testing different diagnostic methods.      Improve care -  5. Develop a database of PD outpatients in sites in the different countries to enable description of their characteristics.   6. Look at the effectiveness and side-effects of preparations of Mucuna pruriens (MP), a tropical plant, compared to Levodopa (standard drug treatment) in Tanzania. Evidence from an on-going Ghana study suggests MP is affordable, effective and side-effects are limited.  7. Assess the response to drug treatment, with low-cost home monitoring with wearable movement sensors in PwP who consent.    8. Work with patient and carer support groups to understand lived experience, raise public awareness via standard media techniques and social media.  9. Collaborate with the Investigators on a large genetic projects to collect blood, saliva and stool samples for genetic analyses.

Work with patient and carer support groups to understand lived experience, raise public awareness via standard media techniques and social media. 9. Collaborate with the Investigators on a large genetic projects to collect blood, saliva and stool samples for genetic analyses.

title: AI-powered language interpretation: Assessing impact on care delivery in primary care triage settings.
abstract: Theme addressed: AI in primary care.   NHS England guidance states: “patients should be able to access primary care services in a way that ensures their language requirements do not prevent them receiving the same quality of healthcare as others.”1  Language barriers contribute to health inequalities.2  Patients experiencing language barriers have difficulty registering with a GP, accessing urgent care, explaining their problems, and understanding what their doctor says.3  They are more likely to have poorer patient experiences and poorer overall health.4  GPs address this by contracting third-party interpreters. However, these services are beset with issues which impact patient demand and GP triage capacity:         In-person interpreters require arrangements to be made in advance.       Telephone interpreting wait times are often long (in severe cases up to 30 minutes).       They necessitate longer appointment times, reducing overall capacity.       There is a limited availability of interpreters.       Accidental scheduling conflicts are common.       Last-minute interpreter cancellations/delays lead to wasted appointments and rescheduling.         Occupying Tier B of the NICE Evidence Standards Framework, Pocketalk is a handheld interpretation device.  Using AI-based translation technology, it communicates in 82 languages by detecting speech and providing instant translations audibly through a speaker and visually on a screen.5  Holding sole UK healthcare commercialisation rights to Pocketalk, we aim to address these challenges.  Pocketalk has been successfully deployed in sectors such as tourism, refugee support6 and education.7 However, its suitability, effectiveness and impact in healthcare settings are unproven.  Provisional patient and clinician engagement did occur during the pandemic, when 100 devices were donated to NHS providers (including primary care), with positive outcomes.  Working with patients and wider public to develop a safe and effective usage protocol and design a representative study, we now seek to build on this foundation by generating formal real-world evidence of Pocketalk's healthcare impact. If successful, this will support widespread use.
